speechtext: On the Orders of the Day being called:

I wish to cal! the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a return which was ordered by the House on March 23, 1914, and laid on the table yesterday, which purported to show the amount expended in public works in Antigonish county since October 11, 1911. That return is grossly inaccurate. It states that the amount expended since October, 1911, was $75,797.50. When I looked at that first, I thought a mistake had been made in the copying, and that the correct amount was $7,597, which would be more nearly correct than $75,000. I observe that places are mentioned in this return that are not in Antigonish county at all-Battery Point, for instance, and other places. I observe also that the return states that amounts [DOT]of $21,094.97 and $1,315.93 were expended since 1911 for Antigonish public buildings. No question was asked about public buildings; the question was with regard to public works. That statement, however, is grossly inaccurate, beca/use that money was expended, not since 1911, but six or seven years ago, and why it was put in the return I do not know. I observe also that the return states that an amount of $13,130 for Breen's Pond was expended since 1911, whereas that work was performed before 1911. All through the return is inaccurate, and I draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to this fact so that the matter may be corrected before his Estimates are brought up for consideration. The Minister of Public Works may remember that on December 28, 1912, just on the eve of an election in Antigonish county, a promise of $205,000 for public works in that county was made in a letter addressed to Senator Girroir.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I do not think it is in. order for the hon. member to go into these matters at this stage.

I am simply explaining to the minister that possibly the error crept in through some of the officials of his department having had in mind the letter in which the promise Of the expenditure of $205,000 upon public works in Antigonish county was made. Of course, the money was not expended, as promised. The Minister of Public Works gold-bricked the people on that occasion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is certainly exceeding .his rights.

I wish to ask the Minister of Public Works if he intends to try to make the Antigonish people -believe that $75,000 was given them during the past year, when as a matter of fact only a fractional part of it was expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works
speechtext: I did not take the trouble to -read the report, but simply brought down what was given me by the officers of the department. I shall be glad to draw their attention to the statements which my hon. friend has made in regard to inaccuracies, and if such inaccuracies have crept in, I will endeavour to see that they are corrected.

Without reading to the House what has been published in the Montreal papers, I would ask the Minister of Public Works if it is true that a dam is to be built a little above Montreal ^ at a place called Heron Island. I understand that the Waterways Commission, appointed to inspect and report upon the water situat.on above the harbour of Montreal, has not yet filed its final report. Eut

for the last few days it has been stated in the press that a certain company has obtained power from the Government to build a dam near Lachine rapids and a power house on Heron Island. It is said that a contract has been given amounting to $2,500,000. Is that item correct and has the Waterways Commission approved of this project?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works

There is no truth in

I am satisfied it is absolutely incorrect, because I have had several applications in connection with dams and the development of water-powers there, but have invariably given the same answer that nothing could be done until we had the report of the Waterways Commission.

I do not wish to contradict the statement of the minister, but for his information I would say that, in an interview, Mr. W. D. Powell, a director of the company, stated that a company had been incorporated, and that their first expenses in connection with their development would amount to over $6,000,000, and he seems to take it for granted that the company will do the work. Of course, if the hon. minister says no, I presume that is an end to the matter.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. L, P. Pelletier (Postmaster General) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Act and the amendments thereto so as to provide that the minimum salary of clerks in city post offices, the offices of post office inspectors, the offices of superintendents of railway mail service, and the money order exchange office, shall be $600 on appointment; and that the annual increase for any such clerk shall be increased to $100 a year; and that if the salary of any temporary or permanent clerk in the said offices is on the 1st April, 1914, less than $600 it shall forthwith be increased to that amount; and that the salary of any person who may be employed temporarily in any of the said offices for a period of not more than one year, who has not passed the required examination, shall be at the rate of $600 a year.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Two important changes are proposed. First, it is proposed to raise the initial salary, which is now $500, to $600. The other important feature is in regard to the annual increase in salaries. At present a clerk starting at $500 gets an annual increase of $100 a year up to $800, but after reaching that figure the increase is only $50 a year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Up to what
point?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: From $800 to $1,000 in the one case, and from $1,000 to $1,800 in the other.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Are these
clerks under the Civil Service?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
All are under the Civil Service-applying to the outside service. v
&ir \VI LI RID LAURIER:	As I understand it, the only change .proposed is that instead, of starting at $500 a year and increasing by $50 annually, a clerk starts at $600, with a yearly increase of $100 until he reaches the maximum of $1,800.
lili. PELLETIER: Yes. I see no reason why the salaries should not increase by $100 a year after the $800 point is reached.

Has the minister any temporary clerks who have been in his employ for more than one year without passing an examination? This resolution says that the salary shall be raised to $600 in the case of those employed temporarily

for a period of not more than one year, and it occurred to me that the minister might have some temporary clerks employed for more than one year .

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Temporary clerks cannot be employed for more than one year; the Auditor General would not pay them. The temporary clerks now in the service at $500 a year will receive $600, the same as the permanent clerks. It is intended to raise the salary on appointment of both permanent and temporary clerks from $500 to $600 per annum.
From the commencement of their service, or from the time the Act comes into force?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
From the 1st April,
1914. All these matters will be better understood when the Bill is before the House.

I do not rise to offer
any objection. On the contrary, I think the minister is to be commended in view of the high cost of living, high rents, and so on, for increasing the modest salaries of postal employees. Some years ago I took upon myself to give them an increase according to circumstances. I think the hon. gentleman is justified in giving to these faithful employees the same benefits that other classes of employees are receiving. I do not think the country would begrudge the postal employees even a little bigger raise. One point to which I would like to call attention is the fact that the Government has not yet decided whether the outside service is to be put on the same footing as the inside service. It is true that a certain class of employees in the outside service have to pass an examination, but it is not the same kind of examination as is provided by the Civil Service Commission for the inside service. I think the time has come for the Government and Parliament to take a bold stand on this question, and in saying that I think I voice the feelings of all the members of this House, particularly members who sit on your right, Mr. Chairman, as they are most called upon to find positions for their constituents in the Civil Service. Unquestionably the law which was passed some years ago on the inspiration of the Hon. Mr. Fisher, instituting a system of competitive examinations for the inside service, was an excellent law. To-day, members of Parliament and ministers of the Crown can say to all applicants that they have to submit to the law and pass the examination set by the Civil Service Commission before they can
be appointed to the Civil Service. In that way you secure a better service than has hitherto existed. We all know that if in Great Britain they have an excellent civil service,' it is due to their system of competitive examination. I believe that the Hon. Mr. Fisher has no greater title to fame than that he secured such a system for the inside service. In England, no minister of the Crown is hunted by applicants, as we are hunted in this country, because it is a matter of course that all applicants must go before the board of Civil Service commissioners and pass an examination. That is the reason why England has the best civil service in existence. We have adopted that system for the inBide service at Ottawa. Why not extend the principle and bring the outside service under that law? I am quite sure that my hon. friends on the other side of the House, as well as my hon. friends on this side, would favour that. I quite agree that it is not necessary to subject a postmaster who receives $50, $100, or $200 a year to an examination. But for the postal employees in the large cities lilte Ottawa, Montreal, Winnipeg, Toronto, Quebec, Halifax and St. John, and for the customs and inland revenue officers in the large centres, why would it not be a good thing to establish a system of competitive examination? That sentiment exists in the country to-day. The result of the present system is that you do riot get the best men. Since the establishment of the competitive system in the inside service we do not hear of any criticism about the Civil Service.

Suppose a person is to be appointed as assistant in the post office in the town where I live, and I happen to know a man who is a cripple and who can efficiently do the work of the post office, but who is not able to do hard work, would my hon. friend propose to have taken away from me the right of recommending him for the position and have the matter sent to Ottawa for decision? He might have passed the examination, but the fact that he was a cripple and unable to do hard work would not prevail, while the community in which he lived would know that he was admirably qualified for the position.

Of course, my hon.
friend gives a special instance which is only an appeal ad misericordiam. Besides I do not know the population of the place mentioned by my hon. friend.

Let it happen
anywhere.

imj

That would, of course, depend upon the population and the business of the post office. . I would classify these post offices. But if we had a competitive system, say, for the Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa, Calgary and Winnipeg post offices, would it not be better for the service? The Post-master General and the Minister of Customs know that all the difficulties and weaknesses in the service proceed from the fact that under the present system they are imposed upon by political friends in these different cities. This system of com

pet-itive examination exists in other countries. It exists in the United States. No congressman to-day has the right, as he had some years ago, to impose his choice on the Postmaster General of the United States. They have extended the system from the inside to the outside service, and what some 3rears ago was the shame of the public service in that country, has now become, I am pleased to say, its pride. The United States have reformed completely their civil service, both inside and outside, and we could well afford to imitate them in that regard. I shall reserve to myself the right to add some remarks upon the subject when the Bill of my hon. friend the Postmaster General is before the House. The sentiment for this reform is ripe in the country. The public think that the time has come when all public servants of a certain class- I am not speaking of the extreme lower grades-ought to pass a competitive examination.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: You mean clerks?
Yes.
Will this resolution or Bill affect the salaries of officials entering the Post Office Department in Ottawa?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: This is a Bill for the outside service.
Will the salary of a man -entering the Post Office Department in Ottawa still remain at $500?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes.
'Mr. NESBITT: Will the minister, when he brings down his Bill, give us some idea of the number of people who are affected by it?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes, my officers will
be here when the Bill is before the House.
And the amount involved?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
And the amount involved.
Resolution reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. L. P. Pelletier (Postmaster Genera]), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution. Mr. Blondin in the Chair :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Post Office Act, and to provide (a) that the minimum salary of railway mail clerks appointed on probation shall be at the rate of $600 a year, and on confirmation shall he at the rate of $700 a year, with annual increases of $100 thereafter until the maximum of $1,400 is reached; (b) for the temporary employment of railway mail clerks for a period of not more than one year at a salary of $600 and mileage allowance; (c) for the appointment of temporary railway mail clerks as permanent clerks with a salary not exceeding that which they received as such temporary clerks, and eligible for the usual annual increases for the period from the date of their appointment until their salaries amount to $1,000, but not eligible for an increase above $1,000 until they pass the qualifying examination; (d) that if the salary of any railway mail clerk, temporary or permanent, is on the 1st April; 1914, less than $600, it shall forthwith he increased to that amount.

Would my hon. friend
the minister explain the procedure by which he proposes to turn temporary clerks into permanent ones?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We are not turning
temporary clerks into permanent ones We are simply dealing with their salaries.

What does subsection
C mean?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
This resolution is
simply doing for the railway mail clerks what the preceding resolution has done for the employees in the city post offices in the railway mail service, and in the money order exchange offices. We are increasing their initial salaries from $500 to $600, and are providing for an annual increase of $100 instead of $50 when the salary reaches $800, rising to $1,400. That is the sole object of the resolution. We have no right to employ railway mail clerks for' more than one year in a temporary capacity. If at the end of the year they have

not passed the examination, we cannot employ them any longer.

Cannot you employ
them over again in a temporary capacity?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We cannot do that
under the law. The Auditor General would not sign the salary cheques.

Could you not dismiss
them, and then next day reappoint them in a temporary capacity?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: No.

The trouble is that the examinations for railway mail clerks are far too severe. What is required from a railway mail clerk is common sense, good education, sobriety and honesty. In certain provinces my hon. friend must experience very great difficulty in securing railway mail clerks. In the provinces west of the Great Lakes, it is true that they receive 15 per cent above the salaries paid elsewhere. In my day I had great difficulty in getting proper service in that respect, because the salary is not high enough and the examinations required from railway mail clerks are equal to the examinations required from university students. You cannot get a young university student to devote his life to the work of a railway mail clerk. It is very tedious work, it is not always very healthy, and it is at times very risky. I would suggest that my hon. friend amend the regulations so as to make the examinations required from railway mail clerks less difficult than at present. He is quite right in taking on permanently a temporary railway mail clerk who has done good service during one year and has shewn himself fully qualified for the position. These temporary clerks are called railway mail clerks, but, as a matter of fact, they are only labourers. They are employed as labourers for a year, and the Auditor General will not pay beyond a year for one who assumes tbe name of railway mail clerk but is really only a labourer.

Has the hon. member
(Mr. Lemieux) read subsection 0? I understand by that section that if a railway mail clerk stays there long enough, his salary will rise to $1,000 a year.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
He does not stay
there more than a year if he does not pass the examination.
This examination applies to the increase, not to the permanency.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The rule is this: The young man may remain in the service for a year.

Will my hon. friend get away from what the rules and regulations may be, and realize that we are passing a statute, and it is a question what is the interpretation of that statute? My hon. friend should devote his attention to that branch of the question, and not to rules and regulations of the past. He says that the Auditor General will not sign the cheques. That may have been the case in the past. Does not my hon. friend think that subsection C, if passed, will be a statute which the Auditor General will be bound to obey?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: There is no question about that. Perhaps I employed a word which did not carry the meaning I had in my .mind. Possibly I should have used the word ' law ' when I used the word ' rule.' The law now is that we cannot continue in office for more than twelve months a railway mail clerk who is on probation. After the twelve months have expired, if he has not passed the necessary examination, he has to leave the service. I used the word ' rule.' That is the ' law.'
What is the new law?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The new law is to
increase the salaries and to keep in the service those temporary clerks who have made good.
For four years more?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the yearly increase?	*

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
From $600 to $800
under the new law by increases of $100 a year. From $800 to $1,400; as the law now is, the rate of increase is $50 a year, we are making it $100 a year.
Any mail clerk can remain for four years without passing an examination?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: He must take the examination if he wants to be kept on for the second year.
This subsection does not say so.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We are providing by
this resolution to keep in the service men



who are there now and with whose work we are satisfied. This does not say that in future we shall have the right to keep for more than one year railway mail clerks who will be engaged later.

In other words, those
who are employed as temporary clerks will never reach the maximum of the salary given to a regular railway mail clerk?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
No. There are two
examinations. This explanation will also answer partly my hon. friend from Rou-ville (Mr. Lemieux). In the first place, the man goes in without examination. He cannot be kept for more than a year. In order to be appointed he must pass the preliminary examination. This is very easy, calling for only elementary qualifications, such as ability to read and write and a knowledge of the four elementary rules of arithmetic. But the employee cannot have a salary of over $1,000 unless he passes the qualifying examination.

What machinery is it
by which the man, at the end of the year's probation, is changed from a temporary clerk into a permanent clerk? Is it at the discretion of the minister to make the selection, or is the passing of the examination' sufficient?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Both. He must pass the examination, but, even though he may pass the examination, if his services have not been found satisfactory, the minister is not obliged to appoint him.

The minister has said
that section C applies only to clerks now in the employ of the department and that it is not intended to apply to those hereafter appointed. In that ease this section should be amended by some such qualifying words as ' now in the service of the department ' after the expression ' temporary railway mail clerks.' Otherwise it would be open to the minister to appoint temporary clerks, keep them for four years, and raise them to $1,000; and in this way he could saddle on the department a large number not qualified.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I think there is a
good deal in what the hon. gentleman says. This resolution does not exactly express the idea. But I have the proposed Bill before me, and I think it is much clearer.

We have not the Bill
before us. Would the minister read it?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
It says:
A person who has not passed the required Civil Service examination may be employed as a temporary railway mail clerk for a period of not more than one year.
That makes it clear.
Mr. C'ARVELL:	Yes, but then section
C qualifies this broad statement that he cannot be employed for more than a year. Under this section the minister has power to advance him by $100 a year and keep him for four years.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I admit that that construction is possible when you read the resolution. But when you read the Bill-
Will the hon. minister send the Bill over? We have net a copy.
The change is automatic-

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
He is not appointed
until after one year's probation. After that probation, if he passes the preliminary examination, an Order in Council is passed putting him on. Then he advances automatically by $100 a year until he reaches $1,000 a year.

Then, if he passes the
qualifying examination he is put on a par with the other railway mail clerks?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes.
What is the number of the Bill?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It has no number; it has not yet been introduced. We are still on the resolution, and that is why I suggest that we should leave the discussion until we are in Committee on the Bill. W'e can go into the matter fully at that stage. In the meantime I will call the attention of the officers of the department to the remarks that have been made. I wish to have this matter made clear myself.
I beg pardon; I thought * we were in Committee on the Bill.

I wished to satisfy my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) that I
4 p.m. was right. In view of the very difficult examination to which the railway mail clerks are subjected, the Postmaster General is obliged at times to take temporary mail clerks. They are purely and simply labourers, and have a labourer's stipend and cannot advance unless they show that they have the necessary qualifications. According to this pro-

posed plan, they will be appointed at $600 a year and will advance by $100 a year until they reach $1,000. Then, if they pass the qualifying examination, they will be on a par with the regular mail clerks and can reach a maximum of $1,400 a year.

I quite agree with my
hon. friend from Rouville. But I have seen some of these examinations and they are the greatest farce ever known. What difference does it make in the appointment of a railway mail clerk whether he can tell what the capital is of some state in China or Siam?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is mistaken; the railway mail clerks are not subjected to these ridiculous questions.

I have seen the questions and some of them seem to me ridiculous. The proper course for the Postmaster General is to change the examination, and not to take power to himself to drive a coach-and-four through the Civil Service Act. If the examination were put upon a reasonable basis, I do not think there would be much difficulty in getting the proper number of qualified men. The qualifications a man should possess in order to be an efficient railway mail clerk include a knowledge of English, ability to read writing of almost any kind, and an intimate knowledge of the geography of his own country and of many other countries in the world. It may take a year for a man to study up what he needs to know. But I would suggest that the minister should simplify the examination, boil it down to the necessities, and not take too much power to himself.

speechtext: Hon. MARTIN BURRELL (Minister of Agriculture) .moved the second treading of Bill No. 112, to regulate the manufacture and sale of dairy products and to prohibit the manufacture and sale of butter substitutes.

Subsection b of section 5 of this Bill absolutely prohibits the remelting, re-clarifying or re-churning of any kind of 'butter. It is a very common practice to have butter brought from the dairy and taken to the factories and re-churned. A better article is turned out, and the butter is put up in more attractive packages. Will 
the minister tell us why the change is being made?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This Bill is, to a large extent, a revision of part 8 of the Inspection and Sales Act, which was a consolidation of the various dairy Acts passed between 1886 and 1896. Some of the provisions of the Bill are taken out of the Inspection and Sales Act as it was thought to be much better to have a separate Bill dealing entirely with dairy .products. In the interpretation clause of the Bill, section 3, are certain provisions which are necessary for clearness, and which have covered new products which have come into existence in connection with the dairy business since the passing of the first Act. Section 4 corresponds with sections 284, 285 and 287 of the old Acts, and covers in addition, milk powder or casein manufactories, milk or cream shipping stations, and milkbottling establishments. As the law stands at present no prosecution can be made for supplying adulterated milk to these establishments, as they are not mentioned in the Act. Section 5, to which my hon. friend particularly refers, is a re-drafting of sections 298 and 299 of the Inspection and Sales Act. The word ' oleomargarine ' is put in paragraph a, and paragraphs b and c replace section 299 of the Inspection and Sales Act. Section 298 of the original Act is as follows:
No person shall manufacture, Import into Canada, or offer, sell, or have in his possession for sale any oleomargarine, butterine, or other substitutes for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream.
Section 299 is as follows:
No person shall mix with butter any acid, alkali, or chemical or any substance whatever, which is introduced or used for the purpose or with the effect of causing the butter to absorb water or any part of milk or cream; or manufacture, or import into Canada,/ or offer, sell, expose or have in his possession for sale any such mixed butter, any renovated butter or process butter.
That is the butter referred to by my hon. friend which is made over again by churning. With the old section on the statute book, many dishonest dealers throughout the country learned how to add water to butter without the use of any acid, alkali or other chemical substance; and the courts held that, although we might prove that there was 25 per cent or 30 per cent of water in the butter in excess of the legal limit of 16 per cent, we must also prove that an acid, alkali or other chemical substance was used. The result was that, especially in Montreal, a lot of butter was re-

churned and water added without the use of chemicals or acids, and the courts practically refused to convict because there was no proof of these substances having been added. In many cases thousands of dollars have been made by men who rechurned butter and renovated it so that it contained 40 per cent or 45 per cent of water. This was not only a manifest injustice to the producers, but a glaring fraud on the consumers, and it added to the high cost of living. We have therefore put in subsection c, which is as follows:
Melt, clarify, refine, rechurn, or otherwise treat butter to produce what Is generally known as ' process ' or * renovated ' butter, nor add any milk or cream to butter.
There may be something in what my hon. friend says about not allowing people to reehum butter; but if my hon.-friend knew what a business is made of the manufacture of this process butter, he would see that this is the only way of reaching the abuse.

I am afraid my hon.
friend has not paid due regard to the condition of affairs in the drafting of the Bill, because subsection c makes it a criminal offence for any person to-
-melt, clarify, refine, rechurn, or otherwise treat butter to produce what Is generally known as * process ' or * renovated ' butter, nor add any milk or cream to butter.
Subsection k of the interpretation clause defines renovated butter as follows:
' renovated butter ' or ' process butter ' means any butter which has been melted, clarified, refined or rechurned;
If a man rechurns butter without adding water to it, this would make it a crime; it is a crime if he attempts to remodel it in any way. I quite understand that if renovated butter were defined to mean butter with more than 16 per cent of water, it would be all right; but unfortunately subsection k does not say that renovated butter has any specified quantity of water in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will find that commercially there will not be much difficulty of the kind he suggests, because the amount of butter that would be so treated would be infinitesimal. There is probably something in what my hon. friend says, but the matter can be threshed out in the committee. The main provisions of the Bill have been gone over carefully by the parliamentary counsel and the commissioner of dairying. It is my wish to refer the Bill to the Agricultural Committee,
so that the sections may be thoroughly discussed there.

Mr. Chairman, this revision of part 8 of the Inspection and Sales Act, such as amended by chapter 35 of the statutes of 1908, is quite timely, and the more so at a moment when all efforts are being directed towards the improvement of our dairy industry, and as the old law had proved inadequate, I congratulate the hon. the Minister of Agriculture upon having remodeled it to suit the time and present needs. Therefore I heartily approve of this Bill, and 'let me say that it is not in a carping spirit and as a fault-finder that I have taken the floor; on the contrary, I should like to still more improve the Bill by affording the provincial authorities the advantage of operating under this Act. As the law stands, the officers of the Dominion Department of Agriculture are the only ones who have jurisdiction and can exercise the powers conferred by this Act, while the provincial departments of agricure which also possess a thorough organization such as schools for inspectors, lecturers, etc., with a view to the constant development of dairying, have no legal means enabling them to validate their legal proceedings.
True, they have their local regulations, but those regulations are only worth what they are worth and before the law they have no value, as all matters coming within the subject-matter of trade and commerce are exclusively assigned to the Dominion.
Formerly, the Dominion Government had in their employ district analysts who are sent around here and there. Their services were seldom required in those days.
The dairy industry was then in its initial stage; but when it was given a strong impetus and the farmers realized that they would benefit by carrying on dairying on a larger scale, the provincial governments did not wait for the Government officers of the Dominion Department of Agriculture; they set out on organizing themselves with a view to improving and developing the dairying business as rapidly as possible, and various branches were created in the provincial Departments of Agriculture, the officers of which exclusively aimed at making their work a success in the dairying line. The Government of Ontario and Quebec delegated powers to associations, the object of which was identical to theirs. It was under those circumstances that the western and the eastern dairy associations

of Ontario originated, as also the Dairy Association of the province of Quebec.
Those various provincial associations, the organization and operations of which have proved such a success, have their respective laws and regulations recognized by their own governments under which they carry out their admirable work among the dairymen and they have an immediate control over all the dairy products in their respective provinces.
These societies have inspectors whose duty it is to test milk as to value, quality, cleanliness, manufacturing process handling in the manufactures, in short, anything coming within the province of butter and cheese manufacturing as also any other article manufactured from milk.
Now, in order to make this Act effective, it should empower the inspectors appointed by provincial governments as also the dairy associations having inspectors under their control, to testify before provincial courts, under this Dominion Act, so that the evidence given by them before these courts may be valid and effective in law.
There exists an anomaly which should necessarily be done away with if we wish to avoid dealing the dairy industry a stunning blow. We all know how apathetic the dairymen are in complying with the rules of hygiene and probity. The duty of the inspectors is to force the refractory milkmen to obey the laws and to show those who are willing to improve their methods the way to progress.
Unfortunately, nowadays, the courts of both provinces have declared to be ultra vires any prosecution brought by one of the provincial inspectors against milkmen in default. I am informed that no such prosecution may be brought without leave of the Minister of Agriculture at Ottawa, and moreover not only must the action be entered by the Dominion department, but the evidence must also be brought before the court by the same department.
Similar proceedings entered against individuals who were discrediting our dairying by their reprehensible operations have been dismissed by the court of justice in Montreal, in the city of Quebec and elsewhere, and among others, by judge La-vergne, at the Montreal Appellate Court.
Now, section 14 of the Bill which this House is preparing to pass into law and the various provisions of which I approve of, enacts:	' The Minister of Agriculture
may make appointments of inspectors and other persons for the enforcement of this
[Mr 1' yer.]
Act '; but it does not provide that provincial inspectors and others may be included among them.
I do not know the Government's mind. It may be that they intend to appoint a large enough number of inspectors to perform the duties of those who already exist in the several provinces. In the province of Quebec they number from 75 to 80, and Ontario has a still larger staff. In such a case, would the services of those inspectors be at the disposal of the provincial De-parments of Agriculture or the provincial dairy associations?
However, would it not be wise to insert into this Bill an amendment empowering all the inspectors holding diplomas or licenses in the several provinces and directly or indirectly employed by them for the purposes of dairying to act and avail themselves of this Bill in the discharge of their duties?
It goes without saying that those inspectors who are already officially recognized shall be authorized not only to make tests of milk, etc., and any other operation in connection with that, but also to test the precision of the scales of the lacto-densi-meter, lacto-butyrometer, pipettes and other instruments in use in the dairy industry. In short, they will be authorized to enforce this Act in all its provisions. In so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, there are a number of inspectors appointed by the provincial Government for inspecting manufactures who are not under the control of any syndicate organized by the Dairy Association, but the larger number of inspectors are under the immediate control of the Dairy Association. Now, under what conditions do these inspectors exist and what are their prerogatives? Let me quote clause 1963 of ' The Revised Statutes of the Province of Quebec,' section XI, concerning the Dairy Association:
1963. The association, in order to obtain a more prompt and complete diffusion of the best methods to be followed for the production of milk, the manufacture of dairy products and, in general, the advancement of the dairy industry, may subdivide the province into regions, in which syndicates, consisting of proprietors of butter and cheese factories and other like industries, may be established.
The formation and working of such syndicates shall be governed by the regulations made by the said association and approved by the Lieutenant Governor in Council, and such syndicates shall be under the direction and supervision of the association.
To such syndicates the Lieutenant Governor in Council may grant, out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, a subsidy equal to one-half of the expenses incurred for the service of inspec-

tion and instruction organized therein, including the salary ot inspectors, their travelling and other expenses directly connected therewith, but not to exceed three hundred dollars for each syndicate. Such subsidy may be paid to the inspector of the syndicate.
The Minister of Agriculture may allow, in addition, to each syndicate inspector, a bonus varying from twenty-five dollars to one hundred dollars. R.S.Q., 75a; 54 V., c. 20, s. 1; 63 V.. c. 16, s. 1 ; 6 Ed. VII., c. 22, s. 3 ; 7 Ed. VII., c. 20, s. 1.
1964. The inspectors, including inspectors-general and their assistants, shall be appointed by The Lieutenant Governor in council and shall be experts who hold certificates of competency from the board of examiners mentioned in article 1966.
Their duties shall be to superintend the production and supply of milk, as well as the manufacture of butter and cheese in the establishments so organized into such syndicates, the whole in conformity with the regulations made by the said association and approved by the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
The Lieutenant Governor In Council may, at any time, repeal or amend such regulations. R.S.Q., 1753b ; 6 Ed VII., c. 62, s. 4.
As tve see by those two clauses, the parties who are entrusted with those duties must have been through examinations and have followed the rank and file required for their appointment. It shows the qualifications of the inspectors for whom I ask the right of operating under this law.
I will probably apprise the hon. minister of nothing new of the important reform in the inspection system to be enforced during the coming season, because the hon. Mr. Caron must have mentioned it at the conference of the provincial Ministers of Agriculture.
So far, the greatest -part of the inspection work has been carried by 68 inspectors of the Dairy Association. Those inspectors are paid one half by the Government and the other half by the owners of factories visited. In order to keep his position, an inspector must have at least sixteen factories under his inspectorate; in no way are the proprietors compelled to have that inspection, it is optional with them, but the great majority have understood the benefits of that inspection and its teachings. But the abnormal situation of the inspectors is liable to place them between their duty and their interests. The Government will wipe out that uneasiness.
' The province will be divided into fifty districts and the inspectors will be paid in full by the Government so that they may enjoy the fullest freedom in the discharge of their duties.
That reform will necessitate an expenditure of $65,000:	$50,000 in salaries and
$15,000 in contingencies, but the Government can afford to spend only $50,000. We hope that this Government will fill the gap and I dare say, Mr. the minister, that I trust your department to place in their contract a sum of at least $15,000 for the help of that inspection.
To make such an inspection efficient, it should be good to insert in this Bill a clause giving to provincial or other inspectors the same authority as that of federal officers under this law.

speechtext: I would move that the Bill be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Similar Bills in the past have been referred to the Agricultural Committee.

Before the motion passes, I would draw attention to clause 5, which reads:
No person shallmanufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, margarine, hutterine, or other substitute for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream.
Some oleomargarine manufactured from beef suet will keep just as well as butter, and I would recommend that the minister change that section so that it shall read that no one shall manufacture and sell it as butter. If it is sold for what it really is, no harm will be done, because oleomargarine manufactured from beef suet is said by the best authorities to be as pure and wholesome as butter.
It is said to be by the best authorities that I know of; and if poor people are willing to eat margarine, knowing what they are eating, I do not see why they should not. I can understand the minister not wanting to have it sold as butter; that

would be fraud. I have seen margarine that was very hard to distinguish from good butter and that would keep excellently.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
If I may be allowed to answer the remarks of my hon. friend, I would say that he has raised a very big subject indeed and one which is extremely debatable. I may call his attention to the fact that the Act passed by the late Administration does exactly what we are doing. It reads:
No person shall manufacture, import into Canada, or offer, sell or have in his possession for sale, any oleomargarine, butterine, or other substitute for butter, manufactured wholly or in part from any fat other than that of milk or cream.
I am not saying that oleomargarine is not a wholesome product to eat, but if you allowed the sale of a substitute looking exactly like butter although not made of the same ingredients, you would require a tremendously large staff of inspectors to prevent men from selling it as butter. They have had a great difficulty in the United States over that, and I believe the general opinion of this country would be against it.

I would just like to say
a word or two.
