stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. Hazen (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) Bill No. 128, to amend an Act to incorporate the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in Chair.
On section 1-land vested in Crown:

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At the last session of Parliament an Act was passed constituting a harbour commission in Vancouver. The commission consisted of three men, in whom was vested the management of the harbour. Section 14 of the Act vested all Crown lands in the harbour commissioners, who had full control over foreshores and other property. Section 15 provided that all the revenue derived from water lots leased or otherwise disposed of to any persons by the Governor in Council should be retained by the corporation and form part of its general revenue. Last session I estimated that the Government of Canada received from these leases about $12,000 for the year. That was paid to the commissioners for the purpose of carrying on the business in connection with the harbour. Clause 14, which vested these foreshores and the Crown property ,in the harbour commissioners, provided that they should only have the power to lease these properties for a period of twenty-one years subject to renewals for subsequent periods of twenty-one years. The harbour commissioners have asked us to amend that. They have found that there are oases where, in the public interest, they think it desiraible that they should not be so limited. They also .think it desirable in some instances to make actual grants instead of leasing the property. I have the statement of one case under my hand now. The statement made to me by the commissioners is that the original Act was found to be unworkable in so far as grants of these lots were concerned. They saw that it is impossible to issue -any grant whatever, and a case or two has been before the Government for some time where the commissioner's- think it is in the public interest to issue grants. For instance, there is one case where a party, -acting in good faith and through years of dump" in-g, moved the high tide mark seventy-five feet out, and on the l-and thus created, er-eoted a building costing $125,000. After the land had been extended by dumping seventy-five feet out in the harbour, other people bought thi-s property thinking that they would be securing not only the Tipa and the foreshore but this expensive building, but they found that they had no title to the land upon which half of the building stood. The line of the original high tide mark passed through the centre of their building, and under the Act passed last

year neither the Government nor the harbour commissioners could give them any relief. We had no authority or power under this Act to give a grant of this piece of property to which they were fairly entitled on proper terms. The harbour commissioners have asked that this section should be repealed so that the ipower of leasing and disposing of these foreshores should remain, as it had been before, in the hands of the Governor in Council, with a provision that before the Governor in Council shall exercise that power he shall ask the harbour commissioners, when any application is made, for a report upon the question, and thus get their advice in regard to the matter before taking action. The Bill repeals the sections of last year's Bill, revests this power in the Governor in Council and eniacts that:
14.	The Governor in Council may authorize the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to grant any portion of the lands included in the harbour as defined by section 4 of this Act, by deed or otherwise, or lease the same for any term or terms of years hut the application therelfor shall he referred to the corporation for its report in the premises.
15.	The revenue derived from water lots within the limits of the harbour heretofore leased by the Governor in Council or the corporation; the revenue received by the Governor in Council or the corporation after the sixteenth day of May, 1913, from any such water lots otherwise disposed of; and the revenue derived from all grants and leases made under the provisions of this Act, shall he paid to and he retained by the corporation and form part of the general revenue of the corporation.
It in no way interferes with the revenue which is derived by the corporation from these harbour lots, but it is thought better that the power of granting these lots should remain with the Crown and that the Governor in Council should exercise it after obtaining a repoit from the commissioners as to the propriety of disposing of the lots.

As I understand it,
power is taken by the minister to dispose of these lots without advertising for tenders or inviting competition, but purely according to the ideas of the Government and of the commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is right; that is being done every day, and has been done every day for many years. All the foreshores belonging to the Crown in harbours all over Canada have been disposed of for years past in that way. The procedure is this:	Application is made for a grant or
lease of a foreshore. The matter is referred to the chief engineer of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, who makes a report as to the rental value, or, in a case where a grant is being made, as to what amount should be paid for the title in fee simple of the properly. That is submitted to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Public Works, and any grant that is made is upon the joint report to Council of .the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Public Works. The chief engineer of the Department of Marine and Fisheries has to certify that the proposed grant will not in any way interfere with the harbour or cause any obstruction, and the Minister of Public Works has to report that the property will not be required for the purpose of erecting public works upon it. That goes to Council, and it is for Council to say whether the grant or lease shall be given or not as recommended by the two ministers who have investigated the application. There has never been any sale by public auction, and I will tell my hon. friend why. Under the laws governing it, the man who owns the ripa, or bank, has an equity in the foreshore. He has not an absolute right to it, and we could not make a grant giving it to him, but if we grant the foreshore to any person other than the owner of the ripa, the owner of the ripa has the right to prevent any one else from blocking his access by water to the land which he owns and which adjoins this foreshore. You would have to have regard to the rights that the riparian owner has in the foreshores abutting his property, and it would be an improper thing, under the common law, to sell the foreshore to some one other than the owner of the ripa, thereby cutting him off from the privilege which the law gives him respecting the property which is abutting his property.

If it were sold, you
would have to sell it subject to his legal rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The result of that would
be that you would get very little for it. You would have to buy out the riparian proprietor before the foreshore would be any good to the person to whom it was granted. Supposing that certain parties were buying a piece of foreshore, they would have to buy the rights of the owner of the ripa in order to get over the bank and get to their own property. At the same time you could not block his right

of way either, because that is a right which he has over the foreshore. But for that reason it is not sold without knowing that a fair and proper price is paid for it. In some harbours there has been a somewhat hard and fast rule as to what shall be charged for leaseholds. Three years ago, in the harbour of Vancouver, the foreshore was valued at $10 per foot front, and the rental was fixed at 5 per cent of that amount. Two years ago in that harbour we increased the amount to $40, and the rental was 5 per cent on that amount. If there were fifty feet the value would be fixed at $2,000 and 5 per cent of that would represent a rental of $100 a year. There are other cases where it is most difficult to arrive at what the amount should be. All one can do is to use one's best judgment in regard to the matter, and have regard to reports from different officials of the department. I thought, when the Bill was passed last year, that it would be better to have this power vested in the harbour commissioners, because it seemed to me that they, living in the city and making a special study of harbour conditions, would be .better able to come to a conclusion as to what amount should be charged.
That is in regard to the powers of granting and leasing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext: You are reverting to the original position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, with the exception that, before we grant any lease, we shall get the report of the harbour eommis-'sioners, as to the value of the property and as to whether it is in the interest of the harbour to grant the lease.

There is also the very important question of policy involved in this Bill, as to whether the harbour should be kept free, and not pass into the hands of private owners. The idea, -in the first place, of giving the land to the harbour commissioners of Vancouver was that they might control the harbour foreshore, and in that way make it public to a large extent, because the chief difficulty in such harbours is that, when the foreshore passes into the hands of private owners, it becomes so expensive that it is difficult to carry on trade in those harbours. 
In some of the harbours on the other side of the Atlantic, such as Glasgow, very large sums of money are being paid to acquire the rights of private owners; and when a merchant wants to use the harbour, he pays a small rental to the Glasgow Trust, and has the use of the hoisting gear and other appliances of the trust. That, I think, is the ideal system. I do not know whether the minister has considered the question of policy or not. It is a question largely for the harbour commissioners of Vancouver themselves. It strikes me, however, that this is a step backward in providing for the absolute sale of the property. The idea is that the property will pass into the hands of private owners and not be under the control of the harbour commissioners at all. Once 5 p.m. the deed is given and a wharf is erected on the property, the property passes into the possession of a private owner, and the harbour commissioners have no longer any control over it except some control over the rates to be charged. The question of policy is the most important one for the minister to consider. When we pass a law granting the whole of the foreshore of a harbour to a corporation, should we allow them to dispose of it, and put the money into the public treasury?
Mr, HAZEN: That is what we prevented in the Bill of last year. We did not give them any power to sell.
You are giving them that power now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The policy of the Government in all these harbours is against selling, but simply to lease for a period of twenty-one years. I have changed the conditions of the lease in the last eighteen months or two years. The old lease provided for a lease of twenty-one years and then for two further periods of twenty-one years at the same rental, making it practically a lease for 63 years.

Is not that long
enough?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is quite long enough. I am telling my hon. friend of the change in that system that I have introduced. We provide now that, at the end of each twenty-one year period the amount of rental shall be subject to reconsideration. The property may be much more valuable. The condition of the law is that if the lessee and the Government cannot agree as to

what the rental should be, then the rental shall be fixed by application to the Exchequer Court of Canada.

Does not this Bill
authorize a direct grant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am just going to explain that. The policy of the department and the Government is against giving grants in any of these harbours; but, like all questions of policy, there may be exceptional circumstances. An exceptional circumstance arises here and there where people have, before that was the policy, occupied partsof the foreshore, have established manufacturing industries and have erected extensive buildings. In such cases, as in the case of Vancouver harbour, we have to consider whether grants shall be given or not. There are other cases where people apply for sites on which to build elevators. In order to build elevators, they have to float large amounts of bonds upon the property If they have only the lease for the site, they cannot float those bonds as easily and as successfully as if they had title in fee simple, and it may be in the public interest that grants should be made. In every case the interest of the public is safeguarded. Before the Government would grant a lease or issue a patent or do anything in the way of disposing of the property, they should get the opinion of the harbour commissioners as to whether it was in the interest of the public that this should be 'lone -what lease should be given and what rental should be charged. As far as the harbour of Vancouver is concerned, for my own part I would have preferred to leave the matter in the hands of the harbour commissioners; but after a year's experience, they have asked us to take it out of their hands.
There are exceptions to every rule and every policy; but the policy of the Government is to give leases and not to grant titles in fee simple to the foreshore privileges in the different harbours. There are a number of harbours where very grave doubts exist as to who owns the foreshore and as to whether the Crown is represented by the federal or by the local Government. The decision of the Privy Council has left the matter somewhat obscure. Their decision is that in those harbours which were public harbours at the time of Confederation, the foreshore belongs to the Crown as represented by the federal Government, but in those harbours that were not public harbours at the time of Confederation, the foreshore is vested in the Crown as represented by the provincial governments. It leaves us in a doubtful state as to what the meaning of the words ' public harbour ' is-as to whether they mean a place actually used as a public harbour before	Confederation, a place where
goods	were discharged	and	taken
aboard ships, and a place resorted to by ships for anchorage and harbour purposes, or whether they mean a place that has the natural and physical characteristics of a harbour. One case is the harbour of Port Arthur, where people have been receiving patents from the local Government. They have started erecting buildings on the property and have borrowed money on them. Then they have found that the title is called in question, and they apply for grants from this Government vfor titles which they have obtained from the Ontario Government by paying tor them. The matter will have to go before the Privy Council again; although the Privy Council, while laying down the rule I have mentioned, have practically said that the question whether a place is a public harbour or not will depend upon the circumstances of each case, and that it will be very hard to lay down a general rule. While the law is in a most unsatisfactory state, the only thing we can do is to administer it according to common sense and reasonable discretion.
Will the minister ask the Pr.ivy Council to clear up this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is bound to come
some day a friendly suit between the Government of British Columbia and the Government of the Dominion. In the harbour of Prince Rupert and in other harbours along the coast this question is bound to arise. It does not arise in the case of Vancouver harbour, because I think that harbour was" resorted to by ships and was considered a public harbour at the time of Confederation. I think the same can be said of Victoria harbour and Halifax harbour. But as to some places on the lakes it is doubtful if they were harbours before Confederation; and there are places that are harbours to-day only by having been made harbours by the construction of breakwaters, not even having the physical characteristics of harbours naturally. Some day, no doubt, and I think it will be an early day, steps will have to be taken to settle these matters.	.

The kind of harbour
that Halifax will be-with a breakwater.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Halifax is a pretty good
harbour even without the breakwater.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	I am not surprised
that this statute comes back for patching up. I have a very distinct recollection of this measure when it was before the House and in Committee last year. I protested against its provisions at that time, pointing out that it was a most extraordinary piece of legislation. But my observations at that time received very little consideration at the hands of the minister; he thought, and the House with him, that this was a first-class piece of legislation. I confess, I never heard of a case like it. There may be cases wheTe valuable property absolutely vested in the Crown was launched into the hands of private individuals, but I have never heard of such a thing. On the other hand, there may be some difficulty in passing a title from the Crown to a private citizen or corporation. But it is certainly the safest and the best way that the title should remain in the Crown, either in the right of the province or in the right of the Dominion, until that title is finally and absolutely transferred. It strikes me as -a most unsatisfactory way that the rights of the Crown should be| transferred to some private corporation and that corporation empowered to exercise the rights of the Crown in respect of that land.
I cannot conceive of such a method working out satisfactorily. But that is what' was done last yeaT. I am not surprised that the minister comes hack and tells us that it is not working out satisfactorily and should be remedied. I cannot conceive of a better remedy than to let the old common-law have sway. When it comes to the question of erecting something on that land, of course, that is another matter. If a private wharf is built on that property, of course, it must not interfere with navigation. An Act was passed by this Parliament a few years ago under which the power to deal with matters of that kind is vested in the Public Works-Department. The Department of Marine and fisheries having controlling rights to navigation, would have some rights of supervision of a work of that kind. But if an interference with navigation can be controlled absolutely by the department governing the matter, what reason is there for vesting these rights in a private body such as a harbour -commission? That is what struck me as so extraordinary last year, and I am not surprised that amend-
ment is necessary. Briefly, what I say is that the title to the Crown property should remain in the Crown, and if it i.s- to go to the individual either by fee simple or lease, the -control of that fee simple or that lease should remain in the Crown either in the right of the Dominion or the right of the province as the ease may require.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (acting Minister of Railways and Canals), Bill No. 122, to amend the Government Railways Small Claims Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-procedure:

I have to confess,
in the first place, that I do not know much about the Government Railways Small Claims Act, never having lived along the line of a Government railway. But I know that an Act was passed in 1910 providing that a Government railway could be sued like an ordinary Tailway. I think it was brought practically under the general Railway Act -so far as a suit is concerned-a policy which, I think, was along proper lines. I notice that the minister does not propose changing the general policy, but he proposes that the -action shall be against the general manager. That is all right; it does not matter who the defendant is in such -cases so long as h-e is -defined. But the Bill provides not only that process shall be issued against the general manager, but that 'such process may he served upon him or upon any other person duly authorized -by him to accept service or to be served with process in such cases.' It -seems to me the minister is placing quite a burden on the plaintiff. For of eour-se he will remember that thi-s refers to small matters-I have forgotten what is the limit.
Mr. MeKENZIE: Five hundred dollars.

Suppose that a -man at Glace Bay wishes to bring an action against a Government railway, say for $5 for killing a sheep. If he has to go to Moncton to serve hi-s process on the general manager or -some person designated by him, it will cost more to -serve the process than the amount of the claim.

I do not think the general manager of the railway ds going to make it easier for plaintiffs by appointing some person in each town or county upon whom service could be effected. I think the minister should consider the advisability of permitting every agent of the railway to be a person upon whom service can be made. In that way the general manager will get his notice in due course, and things will be made a great deal easier for the plaintiff.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
It is true that in 1910 a
Eill was passed providing that suit might be entered against the Government through the Managing Board of Government Railways. In this legislation the amount was limited to $200, and in 1912 it was increased to $500. The only change which is now made is the elimination of the words ' Government railways managing board' 

the board, of course, being not now in existence-and the substitution therefor of the words ' general manager.' I do not think there is any objection to this Bill *other than that raised by the hon. member for Carleton. I must confess that I do not know much about the law, but it strikes me that if the agent were to be served as suggested by the hon. member for Carleton there might be a possibility of the agent's not forwarding the service, with the result that judgment might be obtained before the general manager or his assistant would know' anything about it. The hon. member states that .service upon the general manager is expensive. Is it not customary for the claimant to mail the service to another solicitor, say at Moncton, who serves the writ upon the proper person?

Yes, but the claimant
has to pay that solicitor. I have not a copy of the statutes here, but if the hon. gentleman will refer to the general statutes of any of the provinces he will find that provisions are made for service of process upon any corporation by service upon its agents%at its local office or place of business. It strikes me that when you bring the Government railways under the general law of the land with regard to suits of this kind, there is no reason why the service of process should not be made to conform with the general laws in the different provinces. I am sure that the hon. minister would meet with no difficulty whatever if he provided for service upon the
recognized agent or person in charge of the local office of the company or government sued. That would not be nearly as broad as is the general law in every province of Canada with regard to the service of process, but it would be broad enough to meet the requirements of any person having occasion to make a claim under this Act.
I do not think there would be any delay on the part of the agents so far as sending in the notice is concerned; they usually look after those things promptly.

The amendment which
the minister has introduced is probably due to something which has arisen in practice. If he could tell the committee what has arisen to make this amendment necessary, perhaps we would appreciate better the point raised 'by the hon. member for Carleton.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The board of management
was abolished a year or two ago, and the change is absolutely necessary in order to provide that there shall be a person upon whom the service of writs may be effected.
What about the general question of service raised by the hon. member for Carleton?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
There is no reason why,
under this Act, the general manager should not issue general instructions to the various officers in that regard.
Why not provide in the Act that he shall do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
I should think that the
Department of Railways and Canals would obtain the opinion of the Justice Department as to whether it would be advisable to have an order of that kind issued. I agree with the hon. member foT Carleton that any person having a small claim against the road should ibe given every facility of service at the least possible expense. If this Bill is passed and these instructions issued, the plan might be tried for a time, and, if it works satisfactorily, be allowed to continue. I think it is better to leave it in the hands of the Government to issue an order and to allow the matter to be tried out in that way than to make absolute provisions for service upon agents.

I can assure my hon.
friend that I am not offering this criticism in any captious spirit. If things go well, in the course of a year I hope that we will have the Intercolonial in the western portion of the province of New Brunswick, and as I make a living through the practice

of law, I expect to be called upon to act on behalf of claimants against the railway. I know that when a man loses a cow on the Canadian Pacific railway he has the habit of coming to me for redress, and I assume that he will do the same thing when the road becomes a government railway. I live 240 miles from Moncton.
It means quite an additional cost to the plaintiff to have to make the service at Moncton when he might just as well make it at his own home. In the .ludicature Acts of the different provinces it is generally provided how processes shall be served on any person who represents a corporation. I think the suggestion my hon. friend is making will work out all right; the difficulty is that if the Government instructed the general manager to appoint certain persons who might accept service, then, if the Crown or the general manager did not appear in answer to the process, the burden would be upon the plaintiff to prove that the person upon whom service had been made had been authorized by the general manager to accept service, and there might be some difficulty in doing that. I think that unless the minister puts a special clause in the statute the service will have to be made upon the general manager.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
How has it worked in the
last three years?
I have no idea. I have had no occasion to deal with it personally.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: If the Bill is allowed to go to its third reading, I shall ascertain all about the present system and shall also have the opinion of the Minister of Justice.

I would suggest that
possibly service might be effected upon any agent in charge of any station.

The district superintendent, I think, might accept service. There is a district superintendent for each division of the road, service upon him could be regarded as service upon the general manager of the line. Could the minister explain section 4, which provides for a set-off or counter claim which His Majesty may have against any plaintiff in any action? I can understand how Mrs. Murphy, if her cow is run over on the railway, has a claim against the Government for the value of the cow; but how can the King have a claim against Mrs. Murphy?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The amendment which is
now being made to the section is of course really only a verbal change to suit the change of management. Its effect is that if a suit is entered against the Government railway and the Government have some claim against the party making the suit, against Mrs. Murphy, the Crown could file its claim against the plaintiff as an offset against the suit entered against the Crown.

Suppose Mrs. Murphy
had torn down the gate or fence, then of course she could not win, as she would have been guilty of contributory negligence; but His Majesty would have the right to recover from her in the same ' action the value of the gate by filing the counter claim.
It would be a great hardship in Prince Edward Island if the superintendent on the island could not be served. For a small claim it might not be worth while sending to Moncton to effect service.

In Nova Scotia there
has been a doubt as to how service can be made. The courts are circumscribed by geographical limits and a writ issuing out of a court in Nova Scotia does not run beyond the limits of that province, except under very exceptional conditions. A writ out of the province of Nova Scotia does not run in the province of New Brunswick, where the manager resides. There should be a provision that a writ could be served upon him where he resides in New Brunswick by a proper officer of that place. The arrangement suggested by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) would be more convenient. We cannot get authority to issue a writ which runs as a binding obligation upon anybody outside of the province from which the writ issues.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. W. J. Roche (Superintendent of Indian Affairs) Bill No. 124, to amend the Indian Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

I have received from an old friend of mine, a letter in regard to this Bill, and in order that the minister may be in a position to answer the complaint, which comes from the Caughnawaga reserve, I will read it. He writes:

The earnest desire of the Caughnawaga Indians is that some good may result from our humble request.
The extraordinary piece of legislation (amendment to the Indian Act passed its first reading March 19, 1914), introduced by the Hon. Dr. Roche is too far-reaching and too injurious to Indians to be dealt with fully in a short letter. I propose only to touch upon one of the amendments, 49a of tne said Indian Act, to show how utterly the natural rights of man are disregarded in special Indian legislation, at the prompting of our official guardian.
Evidently the House does not understand the effect of this Act, and its effect is not understood by the introducer, who, as trustee for Indians, should safeguard our interests.
In former days, the Indians were consulted in the matter of a release or surrender of a reserve before it became valid. (Chapter 81, R.S., 1906, sec. 49, Indian Act.)
Recently a large and intelligent Indian deputation called upon the hon. Minister of the Interior, in regard to the Bill to be introduced to amend the Indian Act.
Our petition contained nearly four hundred names asking the Hon. Dr. Roche to ' exclude Caughnawaga,' for a great many valid reasons. First of all, we are Indians in name only; we are self-supporting, industrious, etc. Our people of Caughnawaga are well known practically in every part of the civilized world, and still we are not recognized as citizens.
The basis and scope of our Indian Act is wrong, and injurious to us, because it interferes with our enjoyments of natural and inherent rights.
We have no voice whatever in legislation. We are often opposed to it and suffer from its effect, as in the present amendment now before your honourable House.
I am convinced that the House of Commons will not pass the proposed amendment (49a) or, at all events, make it general, because there is not a man in or out of the House that knows our desires and needs better than ourselves.
I am sure that the Hon. Dr. Roche would not have introduced it had he been frankly and properly informed. It remains then to expunge it. It is due to your honour and right feeling that this be done immediately.
If you do not take any interest in the cause of the Indian, the forces of injustice will prevail, then you will say: Why have we not done so. If it should happen to pass (Bill 114) I hope that you will not think me unfair if suspicion takes root.
Justice is intended to provide for every man in this country whether his skin be white, red or any other colour.
I do not desire to exhaust the reader and 1 think I have said enough. My main desire is to excite humane and fair-minded gentlemen to go further and examine the subject entirely or to insist upon its being examined in a full and impartial manner.
F. McD. Jacobs,
Chief. *
I hope my hon. friend will give Mr. Jacobs and the Caughnawaga tribe the opinion of the department in regard to this matter.
On section 1-to establish industrial schools:
Would the minister explain?

A foot-note is appended to the section which practically explains it. In some portions of Canada there are no schools to which we can commit Indian children. Under the present Act we are allowed to commit Indian children only to those schools in receipt of Government aid. We wish to broaden the Act so as to create any school, a school to which we can commit Indian children. We are seeking to declare any school an industrial school under the meaning of this Act.

Does my hon. friend contend that he has power to declare an ordinary ^country school, say in the county of Carleton, N.B., a school to which he can send three or four Indian children? Surely the British North America Act would step in there. If there is one thing which is pretty well settled in Canada to-day, it is that schools are under the control of the provinces. I am afraid that my hon. friend is opening up a question that may lead to trouble in the future. I refer to my own province because I see by the foot-note that some difficulty has arisen over a couple of children in the city of St. John. As I understand the law in New Brunswick, those children have the right to attend any public school in that province because the Act states that all children between the ages of five and twenty years have a right to attend the schools. I do not think, however, that this Parliament has the right to give the minister power to say that those children shall go to this school and shall not go to that school. That would be interfering with our provincial rights. My hon. friend can hardly be referring to the ordinary schools of the country, and yet the section says so.
It was not intended to.

I would think not. We have in the province of New Brunswick a number of schools that are Indian schools in a way, and there are schools to which the department makes an allowance of money. These schools are not under the jurisdiction of the school authorities of our province. There is no doubt the minister would have power to send children to these schools under the conditions that he might suggest, but I do not see how he would have any jurisdiction over the ordinary school district, or a school within that district, in the province of New Brunswick; and what would be true of that

province would be true of any other province under the British North America Act.
Are these industrial schools supposed to be places of discipline for wayward Indian children?

Not entirely; but there are industrial schools where children are sent to learn a trade and to be made more fitted for the various occupations of life. They are different from what we call the ordinary residential or day school. This is not intended to refer to the ordinary common school or to trespass upon provincial rights. But there are some institutions, like convents, which are willing to take Indian children, and we wish to take authority to commit Indian children to these schools when mutually satisfactory arrangements have been arrived at. It is not intended to force Indian children on any school, no matter what the character of the school may be. When a satisfactory arrangement is arrived at between the Indian Department and the convent, or residential school, in order to maintain these Indian children, they are committed to these schools, which are not the ordinary Indian, industrial, or residential schools.

Is it not desirable to make this section a little more definite? The explanatory note says:
This amendment enables the Governor in Council to declare schools, other than Indian schools, to be industrial or bearding schools and opens the way for the committal of the said Indian children and other children of the province of New Brunswick and other provinces so situated.
It would appear that this section is sufficiently broad to be applicable to the public schools of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and before the section passes I think it would be necessary to make an amendment restricting its application to industrial schools.
It says, 'any school or institution.'

Before coming to the
House this point struck me, and I asked a question about it. I thought that it might create a difficulty. It is not intended "that the Act shall apply to the common schools.

Is there any provision in the Act that, when you once declare a school to be an Indian school, that gives 
you the power to grant money to it ? Section 10 reads as follows:
The Governor in Council may establish an industrial school or a boarding school for Indians, or may declare any school or institution to be an industrial school or boarding school for the purposes of this and the next following section.
Is there anything in the Act which provides that if you declare any school to be an industrial school you have the right to make a grant and have control over it ? There may be something in the Act which would make that section harmonize with the rest of the Act.
When we send a child to one of these schools, the school is in receipt of a per capita grant, and it is declared to be an industrial school within the meaning of this Act.
If I had read the whole chapter through I might have found something that would explain the section, but as the section reads now it appears to me to be very broad.

The particular regulation referring to this clause is the following:
Under the provisions of section 10 of chapter 81 of the said Act all industrial boarding schools receiving a per capita or other grant from the Government for the education of Indian children are declared to be industrial and boarding schools for the purposes of sections 10 and 11 of the said Act.

That may be so under the regulations which the department may have made, but it is not the real question which we are discussing now. We are discussing the powers conferred upon you by the statute. Any regulations that you might make would not affect the statute itself.

If the minister wishes to avoid the difficulty that has been suggested by my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), it might be done by adding these words after the word ' institution ':
Under the control of the Department of Indian Affairs.
Then it would read:
The Governor in Council may establish an industrial school for a boarding school for Indians, or may declare any such school or institution, under the control of the Department of Indian Affairs, to be an industrial school or boarding school for the purposes of this and the next following section.
That is not what we are seeking to accomplish. We could do that under the Act now.

But is not the objection that is raised the fact that we are giving to the Governor in Council power to declare any school in a province an industrial school ? We do not wish to give him that power, but if you limit the Act so as to apply to any school that is under the control of the department, I see no reason why it should not pass.

You might interline it in this way:
May declare any school to he an institution with which the department has made an arrangement or an agreement.
That would be more in accordance with our practice. I will allow this section to stand with a view to amending it in that way.

I wish to say, in regard to the principle contained in this section as it stands, that there is every objection to the Government taking authority to control the liberty of the individual under an authority other than that of the Government itself. As the Act is at present, the liberty of a neglected Indian child can be restrained and the child can be placed in an institution that is under the control and supervision of the Government. That is clearly a restraint of personal liberty, but to restrict the liberty of an individual and place him under the restraint of an institution which is not under the control of the Government, involves a principle that I would object to very strongly. Without drawing the line too tightly, certainly the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), would be very necessary, so that even if the Government did not absolutely control the educational institution it would have such authority that the Government would be responsible for the character of the institution and the care and attention that would be given to the child placed under restraint.
Section 1 allowed to stand.
On section 2-taking lands for schools:
What is the object of section 2?

At some places where it
has been necessary to get certain lands for schools, we have been unable to acquire them, where they have been held under what are called location tickets. It has been impossible to get the persons occupying such lands to surrender them for the purpose of building schools or making additions to 152
schools. This section is for the purpose of laying down the mode of procedure by which we can get control of the land for the purpose of erecting such schools.
What do the words ' location tickets ' in the Act mean?
In some of the reserves the occupation of the land is held by individual Indians under what is called location tickets.
It is not intended to give power to take land other than land belonging in some way to the band or the reserve?
No, not at all.

When will this Bill be taken
up again?
Does my hon. friend desire that it be not taken up to-night?
I would rather desire that. I shall not be back just as soon as the House convenes after the Easter recess; and as a favour I would ask that the Bill be not taken up in my absence.

I will arrange that.
Progress reported.
At six o'clock, the House resumed, and then took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS.

UNIVERSITY OF EMMANUEL COLLEGE. Tlie House in Committee on Bill No. 89, respecting the University of Saskatche-



wan.-Mr. McKay. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

What is the nature of
this Bill?

Chapter 47 of the Dominion Statutes of 1883 incorporated the University of Saskatchewan, to be located in the then diocese of Saskatchewan. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in 1883 there were no provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, but the territory within those provinces was then part of the Northwest territories, consequently the Dominion Parliament had jurisdiction to pass that Act and incorporate that university. In 1905 part of the territory within which this university was located was formed into the province of Saskatchewan. The Legislature of the province of Saskatchewan, whether rightly or wrongly-I am not taking any objection to that part of it- passed an Act creating a provincial university under the name of the University of Saskatchewan, exactly the same name that had been granted to the university which is the subject of the present measure. This provincial Act went further and >
declared in effect that no other university having power to confer degrees should bear or adopt the name ' University of Saskatchewan.' Now, those who are interested in the first University of Saskatchewan are quite willing, in order that there should be no conflict of names, to give up the name to which they were entitled by priority and to assume the name mentioned dn the present Bill, namely, ' University of Emmanuel College.' I do not know whether this is the proper time to mention it, but I would suggest an amendment to make it explicit that we are dealing with the University of Saskatchewan incorporated by the Dominion Act.

That is referred to in
the recital, and the statute is mentioned.

The hon. member (Mr. McKay) might make the motion now. The amendment makes no material change, but merely identifies the university and makes more definite the intention of the Bill.
Mr. McKAY moved that the words ' being the university incorporated by chapter 47 of the statutes of Canada of 1883 ' be inserted between the words ' Saskatchewan ' and ' herein.'
