speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply.
Fisheries-Salaries and disbursements o£ Fishery Officers, including the expenses of the Fisheries Advisory Board, and an 'allowance of $300 to W. J. E. Casey, secretary thereof, $250,000.
Will the minister explain the increase of $20,000?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There is an increase of $20,000 which may be in excess of the amount really needed although it is pretty hard to say. The expenses of the Fisheries Advisory Board are paid out of this appropriation and during this year it is estimated that they will be in the neighbourhood of $6,000. Last year there was only one meeting of the Atlantic Committee, one of the British Columbia Committee and none of the Prairie Committee. Hereaftf- there will be two meetings per year of each committee. It is also proposed to give a small increase to the fishery officers in British Columbia and the western provinces, and

this increase, with those which will have to be made throughout the country, with the 16,000 which it is estimated the Fishery Advisory Board will cost and with a certain amount of increased printing, which it is estimated will be required, will probably bring the amount up to pretty nearly this increased estimate.
What has the Advisory Board cost up to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I gave the figure in answer to a question in the House the other day. I do not remember what it was, but my recollection is that it was in the neighbourhood of $2,000 for the year.
That is what I recollect myself. It is a very small amount. It does not compose any substantial part of this very large sum.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is expected this year
that it will be about $6,000, because last year no meeting of the prairie section was held, and only one meeting of the Maritime provinces and British Columbia sections.

At the time that the Advisory Board was appointed, about a year ago or more, the minister was expecting very important results from its work. I have not been able to learn that he has adopted any of the suggestions made by the board. I would like to know from him of what use the board is to the department or if it is making any useful suggestions and doing anything to help the department in its work.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The opinion of the permanent officials of the department is that the board has been of very considerable value. We have adopted a number of recommendations that the board has made. I have not a list of these recommendations to give to my hon. friend, but a number have been adopted from time to time, and I believe that the board is a very valuable aid to the permanent officials in discussing fishery matters and in arriving at proper conclusions.

The board made a number of suggestions regarding the fishery regulations, and if the minister has adopted these suggestions it would be well for him to show them to the House, because they, are of very great interest to the people engaged in the fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Practically all the suggestions regarding the lobster regulations were 1524
adopted and have been published in the Canada Gazette.
How are the fishermen to be informed as to what those regulations are?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By notice through the Gazette and by notice being sent to the inspectors. Printed copies are sent to the inspectors to be circulated amongst the fishermen. These regulations were published in the Gazette last week and printed copies are now being obtained^

I think it would be well for the minister to lay before the House a copy of the regulations that have been adopted. There has always been a great deal of difficulty about the fishermen getting information on these questions. As far as publication in the Gazette is concerned, everybody knows that the Gazette is not read by anybody in the country except a few lawyers It never reaches the fishermen at all. These regulations are not very often published in the newspapers. At the time that the Fisheries Act was before the committee, I made a suggestion, which I trust the minister will work out, that the regulations made here should' be published in the yearly statutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That was put into the Act.

That will help. But if those new regulations relating to lobster fisheries have been adopted and are now in force, it is important that the minister should give the information in the House so that it will be made known to the country.	-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have had some 5,000
copies of the regulations published, and we are sending them to the different inspectors throughout the country, asking them to circulate them amongst the fishermen, so that they will be familiar with the regulations. On Monday I shall be very glad to lay a copy of the regulations on the table of the House. What the hon. gentleman says is true. It has been almost an annual subject of discussion for many years in this House, to discover the best way to circulate knowledge of these regulations; and the officials of the department, who are naturally desirous of meeting the wishes of Parliament and are doing their best in the matter, have decided that they are doing the best they can by publishing these regulations in the Gazette. They have them printed and send copies of these printed

regulations to the different inspectors, instructing them as far as possible to make their contents known to the fishermen throughout their districts. If any hon. gentleman will suggest a better way, the department will be glad to act upon it. For my own part, after talking with the superintendent of fisheries and the deputy minister after the discussion which took place on the revision of the Fishery Act, I can conceive of no better way of doing it than the way in which it is being done at present.
Does this item include the salaries of officers engaged in the publication of the fishery bulletin or in collecting information to be published in that bulletin?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

In my judgment the bulletin is very inaccurate. It is of no service at all in so far as giving useful and correct information in regard to our fisheries is concerned. I took the opportunity some weeks ago of asking the minister how he obtained the information that appears from time to time in the fishery bulletin. He informed me that it was sent to the department by the fishery officers throughout the Maritime provinces; that those fishery officers did not receive any remuneration for the work, and that it was part of their duty as fishery officers to collect this information and to forward it to the department. We could not expect them to get accurate information under such circumstances, because there would be a good deal of expense involved in collecting anything like correct information on the coast of the Maritime provinces in regard to the quantity of fish caught. For example, in my own constituency there are 150 miles of seacoast line dotted all along the shore with small harbours, in each of which a number of fishermen work. In my constituency there are two fishery officers, one having jurisdiction over about 100 miles of coast and the other over about 50 miles. It would be mere guesswork on their part to state to the department that so many haddock or codfish had been caught in a certain month. They do not know nearly so much about it as I do, because they are not in touch with the fishermen on the coast. One of them lives in the town of Guysborough.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Would he not be
P p.m. in touch with the dealers from
whom he could get information?
IMr. Hazen.]

I do not think so, because, if so, he could get correct information. Some of the dealers have sent me statistics as to the quantity of fish caught, and their figures are so much greater than those given in the bulletin that the bulletin would be laughed at by any dealer along the coast. The fact must be that the inspector in. my constituency who furnishes this information for the bulletin is not endeavouring the get information at all, but is arriving at it by mere guesswork. You cannot expect this man to travel along this coast every month for a hundred miles and see the dealers and send anything like correct information to the department, when he is not paid anything for doing the work. He would get a good deal of information by using the telephone or the telegraph line if instructed to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is.

As long as no allowance is made to him for his services, I do not suppose he is very much interested in the matter. The bulletin is a most absurd looking document. It starts out by professing to give statements by counties. The minister can take up any copy of the bulletin he chooses. It does not give statements by counties at all. Take, for example, the bulletin for December, 1913. The heading is:
Returns showing by counties the quantity and value of all sea fish caught and landed in a green state, and the estimated proportion of the catch marketed or intended to be marketed in a fresh, dried, pickled, canned, etc., sjtatel during the month of December, 1913.
Then, when we come to look at the counties, the bulletin referred to gives the counties of Richmond, Cape Breton, Victoria, Guysborough, Halifax, Queens, Shelburne, Yarmouth, Digby and Annapolis, but a number of counties are left out altogether and there is no return for them. That is the case in nearly every one of these bulletins.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In that month would there be any fishing in the counties left out?

There would no doubt
be some fishing. There might be some counties in which there would be no fishing. Take the bulletin for January, 1913. The same heading appears in all these bulletins, professing that the work is done by counties.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We have there the counties of Richmond, Cape Breton, Victoria, Guysborough, Halifax, Lunenburg, Queens,

Shelburne, Yarmouth, Digby - and Annapolis.

And you have the counties of Inverness, Hants, Kings, Colchester and Antigonish all omitted. That is the season in which smelts are caught in the province of Nova Scotia, and no doubt in the other provinces. The same is true of the province of New Brunswick; you will find that counties that produce the most smelts in certain months of the year are not mentioned at all. Charlotte is the only county mentioned in January, 1913. The counties of New Brunswick where most fishing is done in January are the counties of Gloucester, Kent, Northumberland and Restigouche; and yet no mention is made of these counties. Now, take the cod and haddock fisheries of January. This return shows that there were only 1,100 cwt. of codfish and 8,800 cwts. of haddock caught during that month in the county of Guysborough, the value being placed at $14,575. We happen to know something about the quantity caught in that month. Last year the question was up in this House regarding branch railways, and Mr. Whitman, of Canso, collected some information and forwarded it here, and I placed it on 'Hansard.' Mr. Whitman telegraphed under date of 24th of January, 1913:
Another week of stormy weather has made it difficult for the boats to fish. Landings for the week, 150,000 lbs. of haddock.
Mt. Whitman sent the following telegram to the Prime Minister:
Canso, January 24, 1914. Hon. R. L. Borden, Ottawa:
Your kind reference to the present need of railway conectlon to fishing centres encourages us. Eastern Nova Scotia will show surprising
progress if shipping facilities provided for fisheries. We know you have always recognized this and hope you can arrange to have the matter carefully considered now. Canso's shipment of fresh fish over Intercolonial railway this month will approach hundred carloads. What we could ship with better facilities can be inferred.
E. C. Whitman.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That would include frozen fish?

I do not think they freeze the fish, but ship them packed in ice in a refrigerator car. But, whether frozen or not, this is the amount caught and landed in January, 1913. Now, if you compare the bulletin with the statement of Mr. Whitman, the bulletin becomes merely ridiculous. And the same is true for 1914.
I happened to get similar information regarding C'anso for the month of January, 1914, and I find that the bulletin was just as far out in that year as in the year before. And Canso is only one point in Guysborough, though the most important one; but there are others at which considerable fish is landed. The value placed on fish by the bulletin for the whole county of Guysborough was $14,978. Deduct the value of the hake and smelts and you have $14,575. This means that Canso alone, according to Mr. Whitman's statement, sent out fish to the value of $60,000, estimating it at 1J cents per lb., which is tile current price in Canso. Now, take the product for the yeaT. I have figured up the returns in the bulletin for my own constituency for the year 1913, and I find that the total amounts to only $449,740. But we have the shipments from Canso to Mulgrave to guide us, and these are correct, because we get the figures from the Intercolonial railway at Mulgrave. From Canso alone and by this route alone the fish shipped represented the value of $417,680, estimating it at the market price. This is only the port of Canso. But there are coasting steamers from various other ports along that coast that carry fish to Halifax. Then a great deal of fish is salted or disposed of in other ways. Yet we find that Canso alone shipped out about as much fish as is credited to the whole county of Guysborough in the bulletin. And besides this we have 150 miles of coast with a large number of places where fish are caught. So that there can be no doubt at all that this is incorrect. The fish from such places as Drum Head, New Harbour, Bickerton, Lis comb and Marie Joseph and not reach Canso. They are quite a distance west of Canso and the shipments would reach Halifax or some other market. I have no doubt, from these faets, that the information found in the bulletin is so incorrect that it would be far better not to have it at all. I am not sure whether the minister compiled his return for the year from these bulletins, but if he does his return will be very misleading indeed. I had been under the impression that the returns were compiled largely from the statements made by claimants for bounties, but that is not correct either. The matter was largely one of guess work. All the fisherman cares for is to prove that he has caught enough fish to qualify for the bounty, and as a rule he does not keep any definite record that would enable the

'officials to compile correct statistics from the bounty returns. When Mr. Cowie was appointed and a new branch of the department established to do this work, we all thought that there would be a reform. It appears to me, however, that if the work is carried on as it is carried on now, it will be worse than nothing, and it would be better to pension Mr. Cowie, disband his officers and leave the matter alone. I am certain that I am correct in this matter, and I would like the minister to give it his serious attention. I am not speaking in any party spirit; the minister can see how very important it is that the fishery statistics which we send abroad as to the catch in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island should be absolutely reliable.

The reports for December and January certainly struck me very forcibly, although I am not in a position to say that they were not correct. In Gloucester county the conditions may change and be more or less favourable at different times, but in the Tracadie, Pokemouche, and Cara-quet rivers and in Bathurst harbour, even in the month of December, when the waters are frozen over, fishing may be done with hook and line. Although I am not in a position to criticise, I must say that my attention was drawn to the showing of the return, and, with the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I would ask the hon. minister to call the attention of his officers to this matter.

I should like to call the minister's attention to what is a very apparent inaccuracy in the bulletin of fishery statistics for the month of February last. It is stated in this bulletin that the quantity of smelts caught in the county of Richmond, Nova Scotia, was 6,000 lb., valued at $120, or 2c. a pound; in Cape Breton county, 4,200 lb., valued at $1,260, or 3c. a pound; in Antigonish county, 5,600 lb., valued at $280, or 5e. a pound; in Guysborough, 1,000 lb. valued at $50, or 5c. a pound; in Lunenburg, 800 lb., valued at $80, or 10c. a pound.
I am not going to challenge the correctness of the quantities that are set out here as having been caught in the different counties, because I am in no position to verify the figures, but it does seem to be extraordinary that there should be such a difference in the value of the smelts caught in the same month in adjoining counties. I do not know who the fishery officers are, or who are the functionaries who furnish the information for the county of Richmond,
I Mr. Sinclair.]
but it is apparent upon the face of it that these figures are absolutely inaccurate. Smelts caught in the county of Richmond should certainly be worth as much as smelts caught in Antigonish, and the same is true with regard to all the other counties of the eastern part of the province of Nova Scotia. The smelt fishermen of Richmond county ship smelts direct to the United States market, and the smelts caught in Antigonish, Guysborough and Cape Breton counties are sold in the same market. If those smelts bring seven cents a pound in the county of Inverness and ten cents a pound in the county of Lunenburg, surely the value of the smelts caught in the county of Richmond would be pretty nearly the same. I merely point this out for the purpose of showing the hon. minister how absolutely unreliable and inaccurate this information is, and unless some officials can be found who can furnish information that is reliable to some extent at least, it would be very much better that these statistics should not be given at all.

The bulletin for the month of January gives the following as the catch: Cod, 8,979 cwt.; haddock, 964 ewt.; hake, 48 cwt. That is the catch, as I understand it, in the whole of Guysborough county for January, 1914. I happen to have the correct information as to the catch for the week ending January 3, 1913, and the amount caught at Canso alone during that week was 912,000 lbs.; for the week ending January 10, 1914, the amount is estimated at 700,000 lb., making a total of 1,612,000 lb. in two weeks. Deducting 153,000 lbs. for the three days in December, we have a total catch of 1,459,000 lb. landed at Canso alone during the first ten days in January. If you give the Canso fishermen three weeks fishing in January -and they will have more than that this year-the catch will average 700,000 lb. a week, that is, 2,100,000 lb. That would be the catch of Canso alone, whereas the bulletin reports only 1,000,000 lb. for the whole county. The names of some of the men who caught this fish, for the week ending January 3,	1914, were:	H. Kavanagh,
27,000 lbs.; Pat Ryan, 15,000; Jake Manuel, 24,000; W. Power, 23,000; W. Ryan, 12,000; K. Meagher, 12,000; SamHurst, 11,000; J. Lums-den, 26,000; F. Lohnes, 33,000; G. Little, 20,000; J.Kennedy,20,000;R.Mosher, 16,000; C. Mosher, 20,000; L. Feltmate, 18,000; Ed' Kavanagh, 25,000; J. Hearn, 14,000; Ed. Hearn, 18,000; Thos. Fanning, 16,000; J. Grady, 8,000; J. J. Berrigan, 14,000; John

Hurst, 14,000; George Ryan, 22,000; Matthew Munroe, 18,000; Frank Hawes, 22,000; John Boudrot, 26,000; Frank Goodwin, 15,000; D. Walsh, 8,000; W. Shrider, 17,000; Fred. Rhynolds, 15,000; Thomas Garter, 11000; Sandy Meagher, 17,000; Samuel Snow, 17,000; Levi Ehler, 10,000; S. Munroe, 9,000; S. Hurst, 8,000; John Carter, 11,000; dories and other boats (estimated), 300,000; total, 912,000 pounds.	.
That is a total of 912,000 pounds in one week, very nearly as much as is given by the bulletin for the whole month. According to the statement, the following week there were one or two stormy days and only 700,000 lb. was caught; but the information I have is that the average at Canso alone during January 1914 was about 700 000 lb. for each week. The bulletin gives a little less than a million lbs. for the whole month. It would appear that the officer who has charge of this branch in that district did not ask anybody, but simply sat at home in his office in Guys-borough, thirty miles away, and made an estimate in his own mind and sent a guess to the department. That is the way the work must be done, because if he had gone to Canso or had written to the merchants he would have got this information that I have received. I have no doubt about the correctness of this information, and as I have gone into it in detail I hope I have convinced the minister of the importance of looking into this matter and trying to have it adjusted.
Mj\ LAW:	How are these statistics prepared? Does the inspector or the overseer of the district prepare them? From whom does he get the information. As far as Yarmouth is concerned, the fishermen take very little stock in this bulletin; but I am not in a position to point out where there are any inaccuracies or where the bulletin is correct, as my hon. friend has done. It has always been a mystery to me where the overseers got the information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The system that I believe
was in force up to early in 1911 was that the statistics were gathered together once a year by the fishery officers from the best sources available and they were largely dependent on the returns that were made at the time the bounty checks were being paid. The department determined to get better statistics, and about 1909 Mr. Cowie was employed. In the spring of 1911 the system of getting these monthly returns
and issuing a monthly bulletin was adopted by the department. It is the duty of the overseer in each district to get the returns from the best source he can, from the officials under him at the different places in the district in which he is overseer, or if necessary from local dealers or others. Blank forms for the purpose are furnished. Instructions are given to the inspector to keep an oversight on the matter, to try and inform himself as well as he can and to see that the statistics are correct.
In addition to that, a circular letter was sent out by the department to all the different fish dealers who would be in close touch with the fishing operations, and they were asked to write to the department from time to time if they saw inaccuracies in the bulletin and to let the department know if they thought mistakes were being made, so that the department might be in a position to correct them. I am told by the superintendent of fisheries that, up to the present, practically not a single complaint has been received at the Fisheries Department from any of these dealers. It therefore comes as a surprise to the superintendent of fisheries, who is with me, that the complaint of the hon. member for Guysborough is so sweeping in its character. It would have occurred to the superintendent, as it would to almost any one else-and I isay this without reflecting on the statement of the hon. member-that if such glaring inaccuracies had occurred, even if they had not been especially requested to do so, the dealers to whom these bulletins are sent would have informed the department of the error. But when we consider that they were especially requested to inform the department of any error, the statement comes as a greater surprise. I entirely agree with the hon. member for Guysborough that it is useless to publish statistics unless they can be relied upon; they are worse than useless if they do not give an approximately correct idea of the fishing operations carried on and the quantity of fish caught. I say approximately, because it cannot be expected they will be absolutely correct. There must be some variation, although, of course, it should be impossible that there could be such a discrepancy as exists between the statement of the non. member for Guysborough and the bulletin. I am not prepared, I would not be expected to be prepared to say that the bulletins are grossly inaccurate. All I can say is that I will most certainly ask the officers charged with the duty of looking after the

gathering of these statistics to thoroughly investigate the matter at once, and if it is found that they are nearly as inaccurate as would appear, I think we should take prompt steps to have them made more accurate so that they can be relied upon, and instructions to that effect will be given to the officers. It seems to me as if the statement made by the hon. member for Guysborough is made after careful inquiry, and it looks as if he might be pretty near the mark. I, of course, say that subject to correction, as I do not pretend to give an opinion one way or the other at the moment.
The hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) has referred to the discrepancy in the price of smelt. That might be accounted for by the quantity caught and the nature of the market at the time they were caught. If only a small quantity, practically used for home consumption in the markets near at hand, were caught, I presume that a larger price would be charged than if a large quantity were caught for shipment outside of the province. Those who collect the statistics are instructed to give the market value of the fish at the port to which the fish are brought. Those are their instructions. It is hard to understand why anybody making these returns would think .it worth his while to give anything but the correct market value 'at the port to which the fish, are brought.
I fully appreciate the trouble my hon. friend from Guysborough has gone to, and I will certainly see that the matter is made the subject of most careful inquiry with a view to remedying in future any fault in the system of collecting these statistics.

The fishermen in my county are their own shippers. They ship the fish to the United States markets direct. I say that the statement as to price is a mere guess on the part of the person who furnishes this information. Perhaps the hon. minister has the names of those persons for the county of Richmond.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend the names of the overseers in his county.

I know the overseers myself. They live many miles from the sections of the county of Richmond where these smelts are caught. Inasmuch as the fishery officers are not paid for collecting these statistics, they can scarcely be expected to visit the districts where the fishery operations are carried on, and for that reason I say that any information I -Mr. Hazen.f
forwarded by them to the department is a mere guess. I am absolutely certain that the fishery officers, with perhaps one or two exceptions, do not get the information from the men -who catch the smelts. The discrepancy is so absolutely manifest upon the face of this bulletin that some explanation is certainly in order as to why the information as to price is not more accu-'rate. There is no considerable quantity consumed in the local market and the fishermen of the county of Richmond' receive practically the same price as the smelt fishermen in other parts of eastern Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The fact that these officers do not live where the fishing operations are carried on is no excuse for their giving incorrect dnfoiimation. Most of them live, I presume, near a telephone or a telegraph line and they are instructed to use the telephone and the telegraph at the department's expense.
Would it not be worth while to institute some inquiry as to the sources of information upon which these officers draw?

The county I have the honour to represent shipped to local and foreign markets 382 tons of smelts during the month of February, and you will see by the bulletin that the average price was over five cents a pound. Never in the experience of the smelt fishermen of New Brunswick have they received such a good price for their smelts as this year. I wonder if the hon. minister could give me the reason for that? Their only markets are Canada and the United States. I will tell the minister why the price is so much better this year. It is because the United States took the duty off. The Canadian consumer of course has to pay that much more for what he uses. That has increased the cost of living in Canada and I leave it to the Minister Finance to get us out of that difficulty. Could not the Minister of Marine and Fisheries check these quantities each month with the entry outwards which is made at every port through which the fish are exported to the United States? That would be very useful information to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think the customs returns show that.

I suppose we could pick out the information from the -customs returns, but the Customs Department does not issue a monthly bulletin as the Department of Marine and Fisheries does. It

seems to me that it would not be very difficult for the minister to publish each month the quantities exported and to what country. That would be a check on the values and on the quantities. The price of smelts as given for the county of Richmond is absolutely inaccurate, as the smelts were worth practically 200 per cent more than that on the fishing grounds.
What about Lunenburg?

I understand that the
price there is very high, probably the local trade accounts for that. In Northumberland county, in Gloucester and Kent the quantities are very large. Three hundred and eighty-two tons for one month from Northumberland county gives you some idea as to the value of the American market to the fishermen of that county, especially when it is not a taxed market. By the taking off of the American tax the fishermen of Northumberland county have reaped the benefit to the extent of $15 per ton on 382 tons in one month.

I think the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Kyte) gave the correct explanation when he said that the minister did not get accurate information because he did not pay anything for the work of collecting these statistics. I asked a question during the present session as to what it cost to get up this bulletin and the answer was: for 1912-13, $1,251.78, and for 1913-14, $1,222.15. How can we expect to get important work like this done along the coast oi the Maritime provinces and of British Columbia for the paltry sum of $1,200?
If you want the officers to take any interest in this work you must pay them something. If the minister is going to deal with this question in a proper way he must put some amount in the Estimates for the present year to pay for the collection of the information with which to get up these bulletins.
To whom are these bulletins sent each month?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: To all members of Parliament, to the different fishing concerns, to the newspapers and practically to everybody who sends in his name and asks that they shall be sent to him.

Can any fisherman, or any
person, have them sent regularly if he forwards his name to the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, write to the department and I shall be glad to give instructions to have them sent.

Can the minister give
me the name of the fishery overseers for the county of Queens?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The overseers for the
county of Queens are Charles Young and W. E. Fraser.
Is Mr. Fraser an overseer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I wish to call the attention of the minister to something more or less interesting about W. E. Fraser.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: When I say Mr. Fraser is an overseer I should say that I am under the impression that he has resigned.
When did he resign?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Some time early in February.
Was he ever loaned by the minister's department to the Department of Militia for any purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, I have never heard of such a thing. I do not know what he would be doing there.

Hon. members opposite take a great deal of pleasure, and have a good deal of pride, in talking about the local election that took place in Nova Scotia in February last. The result was satisfactory to them. I had the pleasure of experiencing the presence of this man Fraser in the county of Victoria. This distinguished officer of the minister, on election day, furnished by somebody with moneys which he lavishly expended, maintained an open public house within a few hundred yards of a polling place in a certain district in Victoria county where he dispensed rum, cigars and all other luxuries that science could devise and money could buy. He represented himself as not only an officer of the Marine and Fisheries Department, but as an officer who was selected by the Minister of Militia and sent to the county of Victoria for the purpose of settling the Fenian Raid claims. He told the electors who were looking for their Fenian Raid bounties that he was selected by the Department of Militia and Defence and sent down to Victoria with plenary powers to settle every claim that was outstanding. He went to the extent of offering to pay seventy-five per cent of the $100 claims of some of the electors in the district where he held the public house on election day, provided, of course, that they delivered

the goods or voted for his man. I do not know how much money he paid out in that way but he was well armed, according to the reports, with the necessaries. He assured the people that he was the accredited representative of the Militia Department. I was informed by the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Hughes) that no man was authorized to do such a thing, and that he had not given Fraser, or anybody else, any authority to speak for him in that connection. What I say to the minister I can prove to the hilt if necessary. If Fraser is an officer of the minister I think it would be reflecting a little more credit on his department if this gentleman would at least tell the truth when he went on missions of this kind. I do not think he should have gone at all. I think he should have respected his office more than to go outside of his own county and try to debauch the electorate as he did in the county of Victoria. I do not think he should have gone, but if he did go he should have been paid, sufficiently to tell the truth and, if he had to lie about any department, let him lie about his own department. He transgressed every rule of decent lying by lying for a department that he had nothing whatever to do with. I complain of this conduct on the part of any officer of the Government. I bring the matter before the minister so that in future he may perhaps know that all his officers are not saints when he hears complaints about them and will have reason to believe that there may be some truth in these complaints. I make these statements upon my responsibility as a member of the House, and I am well able to back them up in this particular instance when occasion requires.

While we are on the subject of active partisanship, I am sorry that I have to trouble the minister again,. but I would ask him if, according to the promise that he made on the 27th of February last, he has written to the fishery overseers in the county of Gloucester?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I gave instructions to the department that they should be written to. '
May I ask the minister if he has written to James Doucett of Petit Rocher?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not recollect the name, but my deputy minister was here, and. I told him to take down the three names which were mentioned by the hon. gentleman, and have the overseers communicated with.

Have they been written
to?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I presume they have been.

If they have been written to I wish to inform the minister that the officer at Petit Rocher has paid no attention to the orders of the minister, as this James Doucett has not only been active, but most offensive, in his .conduct towards other Liberal officers along the Intercolonial railway. This man was canvassing for several days on or about the 11th of March and insulting every respectable citizen that he met on the road. I have already said to the minister something to the effect that if he had known this gentleman as I know him, and as I have known him since he was a boy, he would never have appointed him to any responsible position in his department. The man is by nature offensive, and I have not only letters but even telegrams from the most respectable citizens of the parish complaining to me of him on that very day. I have a telegram here dated the 19th March, signed by one of the most respected citizens. It reads as follows:
James Doucett, head man in running around soliciting witnesses against Stevens and interfering in general and I cannot meet Doucett at any time without being insulted for being a Liberal.
I understand that the minister wrote with the intention of bringing that man to respect at least the authority of the . minister of his department, but he has continued day after day to show even greater ambition in his offensiveness. Under the circumstances, and knowing the feelings that have arisen, I would ask the minister to have that man dismissed and replaced by one of his friends. I have no recommendation to make. If I were asked by the minister to recommend any one from among the Conservatives entitled to remuneration by the Conservative party, I would recommend a man who would not have to be complained against. The hon. minister knows that I do not make complaints against any individual in my county without being compelled from a sense of duty to do so. This man, who has been put in this position by reason of the dismissal of another officer, who was dismissed because he was a Liberal, should certainly be dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will look into the matter.

I hope the minister will look into it seriously. It is a grievous matter. I do not complain of the others.
I believe they listened with respect to the

advice of the minister, but Mr. Doucett should never have been appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I will look seriously into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am informed that there is not and never has been any such regulation in the department. The hon. gentleman is aware that in the city of Ottawa
there are gentlemen occupying seats in the city council, one I believe a controller of the city, who are government 10 p.m. officials. In the city of Moncton there have been gentlemen occupying positions in the council who, not only for the last three years but for years before, have been officials of the Intercolonial railway. If the hon. gentleman had been here a few nights ago hf^ would have heard me state that I do not approve of officials of the department taking an active part in politics. I feel it is a practice that ought to be discouraged. It was a practice that was very general under the Government [DOT]which the hon. gentlemen has supported for so many years. I know a great many instances of it. It has existed under both Governments.
My experience has been that, when a man has a position which is his main source^ of living, as a Tule he abstains from taking part in political contests; but when he occupies a position which is subsidiary to his other calling, for example, when he is a postmaster and has a post office in connection with his store, or when he is a lightkeeper but does other work for his support, I find that as a rule he takes part in political contests in support of the Government that has appointed him. It may not be a very desirable condition of affairs, but it is a condition which has existed for a great many years. I think on both sides of the House we shall be talking a good deal that is not very sincere if we shut our eyes to that state of affairs and say that it did not exist in the past and that it does not exist now.

The House must be gratified indeed to hear such a candid admission from the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries when he says there has been a lack of sincerity on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in Opposition. They, in season and out of season, declaimed against the appointment of men to offices because they belonged to the particular type of politics of the party in power. They also declaimed very .strongly against the appointment of these officials because they dared to entertain views of their own in matters of politics, and therefore they dismissed them. Now we have a candid admission on the part of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that, in laying down this rule that Grit officials should not be allowed to exercise the franchise as they

think proper, should not be allowed to exercise the God-given gifts or the right of entertaining opinions for themselves, they were not sincere. The minister admits that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I admit nothing of the sort. If the hon. gentleman thinks that he can construe into my words an admission that a man cannot think for himself, I do not think a5y other hon. member will agree with him.

I did not say that, but I say that the hon. gentleman has dismissed men who held office under the late Administration for no greater reason than that they were Liberals, and exercised their rights as freemen in a free country.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, but there was more
against them than that they were Liberals.
Mr. CHISHOLM. I can produce an instance in the county I have the honour to represent-that of Mr. A. R. McAdam, fishery overseer of the county of Antigonish- who was dismissed for no reason except that perhaps he was suspected of Liberal leanings. The charge made against him by the gentleman who controls the patronage in the county was set forth in a letter written to the minister on the 1st of February, 1912, as follows:
While in Ottawa a few days ago I endeavoured to obtain an interview with you with respect to matters in this county, but you were always occupied when I called, and as I could only remain a few days, I was obliged to come away without seeing you. What I wanted particularly was to know what evidence you require for the dismissal of Alexander R McAdam, of Malignant Cove, fisheries inspector for this county. You will remember that I wrote you some time ago asking that McAdam be dismissed and MacDougall be appointed in his place. This Alexander McAdam has been for the last fifteen years at least an active partisan. He has done everything that any person taking part in hehalf of a candidate usually does. During the last year and immediately previous to the election, this man was chairman of the Liberal organization meetings, was active in calling those meetings together from time to time and was present at most of them. His house was a rendezvous of Liberals and a great many of the meetings were held there.
I don't think that you could find a more active politician in the whole county than Mr McAdam. I should like to have him dismissed at once and Mr. Hugh MacDougall appointed in his stead. I am willing to take full responsibility for this dismissal and can give my reasons at any time. I have charge of tile patronage of this county and am looking after its interests.
Please give this matter your immediate attention.
Yours truly,
E. Lavin Girroir.
[Mr. W. Chisholm.!
When the minister read this letter, he saw that it went too far, that the charges were too sweeping and the accusations exaggerated. So he very properly wrote to Senator Girroir

he was not a senator then-as follows:
February 8, 1912,
I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 1st inst. requesting that the services of Mr. Alexander R. McAdam, of Malignant Cove, as fishery overseer for the county of Antigonish, be dispensed with, and one Mr. Hugh MacDougall be appointed in his stead, and I note fully what you say in regard thereto.
While you explain that Overseer McAdam has been an offensive partisan, you do not say that you have personal knowledge that he has been such.
If you will give me an assurance that you of your personal knowledge know that Mr. McAdam has been a political partisan since holding the said office of fishery overseer, with reasonable specific details of such partisanship, or that from inquiries made by you of responsible persons for whom you could vouch that he has been guilty of undue interference in politics since he has been appointed to office, with sufficient details to establish his guilt of the charge beyond a reasonable doubt, I shall be prepared to further consider the matter. Meantime I shall await a full report from you in the premises.
The hon. minister then was disposed to be eminently fair. He discounted the statements made in Mr. Girrior's letter and insisted that specific charges should be presented. For that he is to he commended. What happened? Charges were preferred

the usual, stereotyped charges,-not specific. These charges came up for investigation before Commissioner Duchemin. Mr. Du-chemin, notwithstanding the express provision of the statute, refused to allow counsel. One witness only was examined, Mr. John Macdonald. The commissioner adjourned the court feeling that there was not sufficient evidence adduced to justify any of the charges against Mr. McAdam. As a matter of fact at that hearing there was not a particle of evidence to justify the statements made by Senator Girroir in his letter. It is true-I wish to be fair-one of the witnesses who was asked to be present did not put in an appearance, and the court was adjourned for the purpose of securing the' evidence of that witness. Now,
I direct the attention of the minister to tho fact that the commissioner himself felt that it was necessary to get further evidence before condemning Mr. McAdam. The adjourned hearing took place some time afterwards, and the witness required was brought before Mr. Duchemin, who examined him in private, according to his own report, but found that the witness had no evidence to give. The only thing the commissioner

could say so far as the evidence it was alleged Mahoney could give, was that the information was unfounded. He so reported, and a copy of his report to the minister I have here. Well, how did they proceed to have Mr. McAdam dismissed? In this way: another letter was written to the minister under date of October 14, 1912. You see, they were all summer scouring the county looking for witnesses to say that Mr. McAdam was a nartisan.
And if ever there was a case in which evidence would be easy to obtain it was in that case, for the fishery overseer had gone 'in the performance of his duty through every section of the county. With the treasury of Canada behind them, evidence could be got to substantiate the charge, if the accused was a partisan. But no such evidence was obtained. So, in this extremity, Mr. Girroir writes this letter: October 14, 1912.
I wish to draw your attention to some facts in connection with the investigation into the charges against A. R. McAdam. As I anticipated there is the greatest difficulty in obtaining the attendance of witnesses. I subpoenaed several and they did not appear.
I was not aware that Mr. Girroir subpoenaed them or that he had the right to subpoena them.
X asked Mr. Duchemin to ascertain from the Justice Department what action should be taken to compel their appearance, and his reply was to the effect that they could not be compelled to appear.
Just fancy a statement of that kind by a responsible senator, having charge of the patronage of the county. The Inquiries Act is as plain as can be on that subject. Mr. Duchemin, whose attention must have been drawn to the Inquiries Act when he was appointed, must have known that, for it is expressly provided in the Act as follows:
Section 4 gives the commissioner the power of summoning of witnesses, and section 5 adds that the commissioners have the same power to enforce the (attendance of witnesses ... as is vested in any court of record in civil cases.
What the senator referred to in his letter from which I have been reading was the non-appearance of Mr. Mahoney. Mr. Mahoney did not appear; he was not subpoenaed in the regular way. Mr. Duchemin in his report says that he had to adjourn the hearing from Malignant Cove, and .said that I stated that Mr. Mahoney was not subpoenaed. So I did. I advised Mr. Mahoney that he did not have to appear until he was subpoenaed and paid his
witness fee. Mr. Duchemin was going up and down the country in the early part of his operaions in the county I have the honour to represent calling witnesses before him, but he did not pay witness fees, and some of those fees are still outstanding. It was only when Mr. Mahoney refused to attend without being subpoenaed in the regular way and paid his fees that Mr. Duchemin carried on his proceedings, so far as witnesses were concerned, in a proper and legal manner and concluded that thereafter the witnesses would have to receive these fees or conduct money.
To quote again from the senator's letter:
This only goes to show the inadequacy of the present machinery for trying these cases.
It only goes to show, I think, either that Mr. Girroir did not know what he was writing about or else that he presumed that the minister knew very little about the Act under which his commissioner was carrying on the investigations.
A Grit with the shrewdness of McAdam usually does his work through others, and in order to prove some of the charges against McAdam it was necessary to subpoena Liberals.
Yes, and they had the whole treasury behind them to subpoena witnesses if they wanted them.
Not one of the Liberals subpoenaed appeared against him.
That is something of which I have a personal knowledge. I happened to be at the investigation, although I was not permitted to appear as counsel. That statement I can meet right here and now. The only man who was asked to attend but failed to put in an appearance, so far as I know-and he was not subpoenaed-was Mahoney.
With the result that we were only able to establish what is contained in the evidence of John McDonald. X think that this evidence should be sufficient to cause his dismissal. If an official can be proven to have canvassed even one voter, there can be no disputing his partisanship. He, McAdam, did not care to go on the stand and give us an opportunity of examining him. This, I think, should, especially where we cannot compel witnesses to appear, be a strong circumstance against him. I firmly trust that you will find your way clear to dismiss McAdam at once. It will be a great relief to me, I can assure you, when this is done.
The sympathetic minister could not resist such a pathetic appeal. The law must be disregarded; the proceedings held before Commissioner Duchemin must be ignored, and the minister must step in and do this
2411,

act in order that relief should be afforded to the gentleman who wanted to have McAdam dismissed. Wha,t was the result? As I have said, the whole summer had passed before the dismissal of Mr. McAdam was effected. Mr. Duchemin adjourned the court from day to day because the evidence that he had obtained in the first instance was not sufficient and he was unable to supplement that evidence. If he considered there was anything in McDonald's evidence he would there and then say: here is a prima facie case against you, which, unless contradicted or explained by you, I shall hold sufficient to justify a report against you. But he turned around at the last moment and said that in view of the fact that McAdam did not go on the stand and disprove-what? disprove nothing, because nothing was proved against him-he ought to be dismissed. Why did he adjourn the case for further evidence if he thought McDonald's evidence sufficient?
Mr. McKENZIE* How d:d he come to be dismissed?
He was dismissed upon the order of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Upon what evidence?
Gould the minister give the names of the members of the advisory board ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are four from Nova Scotia-Mr. Hermain from Shelburne, Mr. Smith from Lunenburg, Mr. Short from Pictou, and Mr. King from Halifax. Mr. King was appointed on the recommendation of the fisheries committee of the Halifax Board of Trade. From New Brunswick the members are: Mr. Russell from Pas-samaquoddy Bay, Mr. Young from Gloucester county, and Mr. Carson from Kent county. There is a gentleman from the
Magdalen islands, Mr. Arsenault. There are no members from Ontario, because Ontario administers its own fisheries. There is a gentleman from Charlottetown, Mr. Longwell; one from Alberta, one from Saskatchewan, and two from British Columbia. The British Columbia representatives are Mr. McIntyre and Mr. Cunningham. Thus there are four from Nova Scotia, three from New Brunswick, one from Magdalen islands, none from Ontario, one from Alberta, one from Saskatchewan, and two from British Columbia.
How many of them are fishermen ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are all fishermen or dealers in fish, or people with knowledge of the fish industry. Mr. Hermain, from Shelburne, is a practical fisherman who makes his living by fishing. Mr. Short, from Pictou, is a fish merchant. Mr. Smith is a gentleman greatly interested in fishing, from Lunenburg. He owns schooners that go off to the banks and he is the representative on this commission of the deep-sea fishing interests, the bank fishermen. Mr. King, from Halifax, is there as the representative of the cured fish industry, which, as my hon. friend knows, centers largely in Halifax. He is the representative of the fish merchants. Originally there were only three members on the board from Nova Scotia, but the fisheries committee of the Halifax Board of Trade recommended that there should be a member of the board representing Halifax, and, that being considered a reasonable request, Mr. King was appointed. Mr. Smith is a representative of the deep-sea fishermen. He has been a practical fisherman, he has fished on the banks himself, he has been the captain of fishing schooners on the banks, and to-day he is engaged in the fishing business, although he does not fish himself. Mr. Young lives at Caraquet, and is familiar with the fishing industry there. Mr. Russell represents the Passamaquoddy Bay district. He is a man who has been a practical fisherman. I believe the gentleman from PrinCe Edward Island has been a practical fisherman. He has been a fishery officer, and the department have a very high appreciation of his fishery knowledge. The representatives from British Columbia are fishery officers. The members of the House of Commons from British Columbia thought at the start that we had better have two men who had been fishery officers, and that is the reason that Mr. Cunningham, who is a
2ilz

principal fishery official of the Dominion Government in British Columbia, and Mr. McIntyre, the assistant commissioner of fisheries for British Columbia, were appointed. Of course the fisheries in the prairie provinces are different from those on the east coast or in British Columbia.

There is only
one of these gentlemen really dependent upon fishing.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: One is now engaged in fishing but two are dependent on fishing. Mr. Smith makes his living out of fishing.
His interest in the calling is different now to what it was when he was a fisherman. He is a fish buyer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
He is a man who has
worked up from the lowest rank. He went off on a fishing vessel originally, he became a captain and he is now an owner and sends vessels off to the banks to fish.

That is what I mean. Would the minister be kind enough to inform me what are the duties of this board, and are they supposed to remain at their homes or to travel around gathering information, giving instructions, etc.?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The board is purely advisory. The provisional arrangement is that they meet in Ottawa two or three times a year. The Maritime section, the Pacific section and the Prairie section meet here and discuss fishery matters with the permanent officials. The object of appointing the board was that it was felt that all the knowledge about fisheries was not confined to the department by any means; and it was thought that it would be an advantage if the officials of the department, many of whom are very learned and scientific men, could have the advantage, several times ,a year, of consulting with men who, while not perhaps having the same scientific knowledge, had a greater practical knowledge of fishing than the officials of the department could be expected to have. It was thought by having an advisory board some good results would be attained. We believe these good results have been attained. We had one meeting in Lunenburg last year and other meetings will be held in other parts. We have in Nova Scotia one gentleman who understands thoroughly the dried and cured fish business, another the bank fishing and another the shore fishing; then Mr. Short, from [DOT]Digby, understands the general conditions. 
'It is thought that these gentlemen, consulting with the scientific men here, can give .advice that will he of great value regarding close seasons, the propagation of [DOT]fish and the best method of placing fish on the market in such attractive shape as to command the best prices. The result, our [DOT]officers believe, has been very satisfactory.

I desire to enter *my protest against the personnel of that commission. There is just one man on it [DOT]whom I would call a fisherman in the sense that I understand the word, a man who devotes his entire time to fishing, a toiler *of the deep.
That is the man that I regard as a fisherman. We have one of that kind, I understand, on the commission, but instead of one at least one-half of the commission should be fishermen. The next protest I wish to make is against appointing all the men from the western part of the province of Nova Scotia. There is no reason why we should stop at the boundary line between Halifax and Guysborough and go no further east. The counties of Guysborough, Pictou, Antigonish, Inverness and the two counties of Cape Breton are without a representative on the board. If there was a particle of sincerity in the organization of this board, surely it would seem that that section of country should be represented, because if my hon. friend looks at the statistics he will see that a great deal of fish is caught in that eastern part of the province. I spoke to the hon. minister, and wrote to him, suggesting a particular friend of his own in the county of Inverness as a fit man for this board. I regarded him as well qualified for the position. He was a fisherman from away back, and made his living at it. I knew that a man of a different political stripe to the minister might not meet with his approval, but this man was a good man, and if he had been appointed he would have been able to give proper attention to the wishes of the fishermen of the eastern counties. I will not take up any more time further than to place myself on record as disapproving of two features of this commission: first of all, the personnel, inasmuch as there is only one fisherman on the board, for I do not regard a man who devotes his time to outfitting vessels as a fisherman; and secondly, the counties of eastern Nova Scotia are left without a representative on the board. I trust the minister will see that these defects are remedied. It can be easily done. He has friends of his own

in all these counties and can easily get men to act on the board. I may point out that last year 35,562.68 was spent on this commission. A commission of that magnitude, so far as expenditure is concerned, should produce some good results.
Might I ask the minister if the members of this commission meet in Ottawa all together, or individually.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The members of the Maritime provinces' section meet here together, but not the board for the whole of Canada.

I am not going to take any issue with what the minister has said except in this regard: he said that Mr. Young had been engaged in the fishing industry all his life; that is perfectly true, but when he came to the other member from New Brunswick he led the House to believe that he had as wide an experience of fishing as Mr. Young. I do not wish to be understood as saying one word against the gentleman who has been appointed. He is a very estimable gentleman, but I am quite sure he cannot be put in the same class, so far as experience in the fishing industry is concerned, with Mr. Young. So far as I am aware he has never had any interest in the fishing business, either as a shipper, buyer or fisherman. I suppose I should congratulate my hon. friend . from Kent, N.B. (Mr. Robidoux) because his county is represented on the board, as well as having a very important member on the Shellfish Commission. Kent county is recognized, I suppose, because of its good work in 1911, while counties that perhaps have larger fishing industries have been altogether overlooked. I thought it was only fair to draw the minister's attention to the fact that his remarks on the gentleman from Kent county, besides Mr. Young, were hardly accurate. I happen to know both gentlemen very well, and I esteem them highly all the same.

I wish to inform the hon. member for Northumberland, N.B. (Mr. Loggie), that while Mr. Carson is not a fisherman and has not been directly interested in the fish business, nevertheless he is thoroughly acquainted with it. The county of Kent is one of the best fishing counties in the Maritime provinces, and the hon. member for Northumberland is well aware of that, because he does a large business in that part of the country. When I urged the appointment of Mr. Carson to 153
that commission, I did it in the interests of the fishermen. My hon. friend will not deny that Mr. Carson is a public-spirited citizen who is prepared to stand by the interests of the fishermen. That is why I recommended his appointment. It may be that his appointment is not to the liking of the hon. member for Northumberland, but I was not particularly concerned about that when I made the recommendation. It would be a pretty difficult matter to suit the hon. gentleman. In order to do that we should have to give him practically a monopoly of all the fishing. He had his innings when the late Government was in power. If we were to appoint an advisory hoard to suit him, we should have to appoint men who are prepared to issue salmon licenses to the hon. member for Northumberland only. We all know that previous to 1911 it was impossible for an ordinary fisherman in the county of Kent, with whom the hon. member for Inverness has so much sympathy, to secure a salmon license. From the northern boundary line of Kent county down to Richibucto about 20 salmon licenses were issued, and the company of which the hon. member for Northumberland is president held 17 of the 20. As a matter of fact he did not fish more than three or four sets, and held the others just to prevent other people from fishing. If the fishermen of Kent county had been given the selection of a man for that advisory board, I am sure they would have selected Mr. Carson.
Does my hon. friend from Northumberland still enjoy the same privilege as to taking out ' licenses?
Yes, he has those - licenses to-day. I will tell my hon. friend this. Any fisherman to-day who applies for a license to fish salmon gets it.

I am inclined to doubt very much the value of this Fisheries Advisory Board. I hardly think the department will get much benefit from the services of a board who are called together practically only once a year.
The members constituting the board as a rule are busy men engaged in other duties and the amount of time devoted to fishery matters is after all very intermittent indeed. A resolution was passed by the Halifax Board of Trade within the past year, I think, and that was a repetition of similar resolutions passed before, urging the ap-



pointment of a departmental officer for each province. I assume they intended that such an officer would be located in a central place in each province and he would have direct control of the departmental affairs in that province. He would always be the real executor of the policy or regulations of the department and would see that they were carried out? He would also be in a position to accumulate, after years of experience, a great deal of information which might toe utilized by the department. I suppose there is some good in the Fisheries Board. I suppose it would hardly be possible for a dozen men to meet together here once a year and not afford the department some information.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They meet twice a year and in future it is intended that they shall meet oftener.

I suppose it would be rather an extreme statement to say that this board could afford no intelligence to the department, but I do not think its assistance is very substantial. I believe that the suggestion elnanating from the Halifax Board of Trade, namely, the appointment of a departmental head in each province, is a more businesslike suggestion, and one which would be more in the interest of the fisheries in each province and of greater advantage to the department than any other proposition which has been placed before the minister on this subject. I do not think that the Department of Marine and Fisheries was ever properly organized for the effective and scientific regulation and administration of the fisheries. F am not finding any particular fault with the present head of the department. What I say would toe applicable to any person who has hitherto been at the head of the department, I do not know whether the department is undermanned or not, I think possibly it is in the way of scientific men, or men who are or will specialize, but I do not think the department is well organized or that it ever was. I believe that the suggestion of the appointment of a departmental head in each province is a good suggestion and one worthy of consideration. I would like to hear if the minister has given consideration to the suggestion which has come from the Halifax Board of Trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That suggestion, of course, has been made on several occasions. We have now in every province inspectors for the different districts and the general opinion of the head officials of the department is that there is very little to be gained

by appointing another official in each province which would be, as it were, simply adding to our inspectors. It is felt that it is quite as easy for these inspectors to report at Ottawa as it would be, in New Brunswick, for instance, for them to report in St. John, or, in Nova Scotia, for them to report in Halifax. But up to the present time it has not been thought desirable to adopt that suggestion which has been made frorq time to time for the last ten years.

I think that some hon.
members have misunderstood the situation as put before the committee by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Robidoux). The licenses that he referred to were held thirty years ago and about twenty years ago the corporation of which I am president and manager was organized and these salmon licenses were taken over by that company. The corporation that I represent received no favours from the Liberal Government any more than they have from the present Conservative Government. They held these licenses many years ago and still hold them, and they are endeavouring to make an honest dollar out of these fisheries. I realize, as much as any man in this House, the importance of taking care of the fisheries and not allowing them to be overburdened. I think that especially applies to the lobster fishery.

What are the
goods like that this company put up?

Write to Fraser, Viger
and Company, of Montreal, and they will tell you the kind of goods that certain people put up. The licenses that my hon. friend referred to are practically licenses that the company have held for thirty years or thereabouts. Some of the territory that the company are fishing in front of cost them a large sum of money. I fancy that there are some shore rights given with these licenses, although the department as a rule refuse to recognize shore rights. But after all they give a preference to the owners of the land in fishing in front of their own land. That is the recognized rule along the shore. I do not think it is always carried out, and I do not say that it is always necessary to carry it out-, as long as the parties holding the licenses have a landing privilege. But if they do not have a landing privilege the owner of the land can prevent them from landing. It is important to have some shore rights. All I got on my feet for was to explain to the committee that the corporation I repre-
APRIL .3, 10i4
sent received no favours from the Liberal Government that they would not be perfectly justified in asking of the Conservative Government. I think that the minister knows enough of my career to say that I could come to Ottawa and ask justice from any Government. While I have always been a Liberal in federal politics I was not a very active partisan until I took hold of my hon. friend himself and worked shoulder to shoulder with him. But when it came to the federal question, even although we were working together, we had to agree to differ and we did differ.

While I admire the
devotion of my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Robidoux) to his fishermen, he will admit that I have some fishermen also in Gloucester county who are dear to my heart. I speak not so much of the shore fishermen, the lobster and salmon fishermen, who are more numerous in my county than in any other county in New Brunswick, but I wish to speak more particularly this evening of the deep sea fishermen whose pursuit is very arduous and who last year were treated in a way that has not been heard of since Confederation in the county of Gloucester or along the north shore of New Brunswick. The deep sea fisherman has to pass with his schooner once or twice through the harbour of Shippigan, and he has been	charged harbour dues
by	the	new harbour	master there.
Whether the conduct of the harbour-master has been according to the rules of the department, I will not say positively, but I wish to remind the minister that it is quite an innovation in: the county of Gloucester; that the schooners have never been charged harbour dues or wharf dues since Confederation, and I do not believe they have been charged harbour dues or wharf dues anywhere on the north shore of New Brunswick. In the county of Gloucester the matter is more important, because 200 schooners leave the ports of Caraquet and Shippigan, every Monday morning, going to the Prince Edward Island banks and taking every summer nearly a million dollars' worth of fish from the bottom of the sea. I would ask the minister to rectify this matter, if possible, and not to impose any taxation on these fishermen. We exempt them from wharfage dues, and I do not see why they should be charged harbour dues.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What harbour?
Shippigan. As the hon. minister knows, all the schooners from Oaraquet, Lameque, Miseou and Shippigan island go out to sea by this harbour.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that fishing vessels are charged harbour dues?
Yes. They were charged last summer, I am informed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
What have they been
charged harbour dues for?
As fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My understanding was that no harbour dues were charged against the-fishermen. There must be some misunderstanding.

There must be some
mistake in the instruction given to the-barbour-master.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I wish the hon. gentleman would write me a letter stating the facts.
I will.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Then I will investigate the matter.

I think the difficulty
about th-e Advisory Board is that the minister has made it political. I am sorry that the minister did not carry out the promise made to the House last year, when authority was given to appoint that board, that he would select the members oLtlie board himself; that he would endeavour to represent all the various interests in regard to the fish industry and that he would select good men. These answers-were given in the House on the 27th of November, 1913. The minister stated most positively that he would make the selection himself, that the selection would not be political.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I did.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Certainly.
And I have no doubt the same is true in regard to the other members of the board, that they were recommended as suitable by some of the friends of the minister.

Before the minister
makes any reply to the observations of the hon. member of Guysborougb (Mr. Sinclair) with respect to the case of this man Fraser, I wish to refresh his memory as to the law of Parliament and of his department as laid down by the present Prime Minister on this very point. This subject was under discussion in this House on the 6th day of December, 1911, as appears on page 889 of ' Hansard'. These are the words of the Prime Minister:
So far as the inside service is concerned, the statutory provision to which I desire to call attention is to be found in the Act of 1908 introduced and passed by the late Administration. Section 43 of that statute is as follows:
* No officer, clerk or employee in the Civil Service shall be debarred from voting at any Dominion or provincial election if under the laws governing the said election he has the right to vote; hut no such officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with said election.'
The words of that section do not seem to restrict it to the inside service. My impression of the interpretation of the Act is that the language is restricted to the inside service. However, that is a matter to which we can very easily determine upon an examination of the earlier part of the statute. Sufficient it is to say for the present that it does lay down a definite and specific rule so far as the inside service is concerned.
Now, so far as the outside service is concerned, the rule was embodied in a resolution of the House of Commons moved by Mr. Hake on the 17th of July, 1905, and accepted by my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was then leading the Government, and that rule is in these words:
' That whilst it is desirable that every official in the employ of the Government of Canada, should enjoy perfect freedom of political opinion, and the untrammelled exercise of his franchise in accord therewith, no official should be engaged or permitted to engage, in partisan work of any description in the election of a representative to the provincial or Dominion Legislature.'

So there appeared to be no latitude for any minister if that law is to be observed. The Prime Minister pointed out that, so far as the inside service is concerned, the statute settled the case, and so far as the outside service is concerned, the late resolution settled it, that resolution being:
No person who is in the pay of the Government shall take any part whatever in partisan work in a Dominion or provincial election.
Any minister who has regard to that as the law has strong reason to make it clear to officials that they cannot be permitted to take part in elections. I wish to point out that not only was Mr. Fraser busily engaged in bribing the electors, but an overseer by the name of William Phelan, who resides in the county of Victoria, was engaged in the same business. He was hand in hand and shoulder to shoulder with this man Fraser in this business, going from house to Rouse offering bribes and bribing the electors to vote for McLeod, who was the candidate of the party. It is only fair that these officials should know that the present Prime Minister of Canada, in a speech in this House on the 6th of December, 1911, laid down the law on this subject, as I have given it. Any man taking office under this Government, particularly since the Prime Minister's statement was made, is forbidden to take any part in a campaign as has been done by these gentlemen.
