I want to point out what I consider to be the ridiculous conduct of the Shellfish Commission when it went around the province of Nova Scotia last year. They visited Orangedale in the county of Inverness, where there are practically no fish except oysters, and they left unvisited the whole of the rest of the county of Inverness, embracing a district TOO miles in length, where there are fifteen or twenty lobster factories. I do not know what instructions the commission received from the department, but it seems to me that if they had any regard to the proper performance of their duties, they should have visited the district to which I have referred. It would appear as if they did not want to trouble themselves; as if they did not want to get too far away from the Intercolonial railway. They reported to the department that they had examined a gentleman at Orangedale, and they left the whole of the county of Inverness unvisited. The Department of Marine and Fisheries seems to have something-I do not know what to call it-against the county of Inverness.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is unparliamentary.

It may be but it is not a personal reference to the hon. member. It may be that I should not have said that, that I should have used some language that would have sounded .a little better. But, when I brought the conduct of this man, Fraser, Who went into that county, lied and represented himself as something that he was not, to the attention of the House, and when an hon. member wanted to break into it and to defend this man I did not think it was conduct that was very commendable. Possibly some language could be used in putting it forward better than the language that I used, but the idea is the same. If the words I used are objectionable, I certainly would regret to have used them, bcause I want to be parliamentary in this House and to speak with dignity and respect-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Then why not withdraw that language ?

-and with as much respect to the hon. gentleman who leads the House as with respect to any other hon. member, because I realize that there is a great dignity in this House and that we can never keep it too high. I hope it shall never be said I ever did anything to lower the dignity of this House; and if the expression I have used has a tendency to lessen the dignity of the hon. member in any respect, I should certainly wish to have it regarded as having never been used.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Withdraw it.
Is not that good enough?
No.
Does the hon. minister think he is going to shove me into a humiliating position ? Is that what he is at ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am doing the very reverse. I have no desire to shove my hon. friend into a humiliating position. I think his position will be much less Lumiliat-

ing if, in compliance with the ruling of the Chair, he withdraws that expression, than if he adheres to his position and refuses to withdraw it. It is the very reverse of humilitating to bow to the ruling of the Chair and to withdraw expressions. It has been done by the leaders of this House and by the most prominent members, time and time again.
If my hon. friend will look at ' Hansard ' to-morrow morning, he will find that the expression was taken back at the very moment it was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Will the hon. member say that he took it back ?
I changed it and said-
Oh, oh.

Hon. members may
laugh. Exception was taken to the word ' dirty.' At once I said I will take that back, and will say that the hon. member broke into a thing that was not clean.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
That is what I said at the time and it was forgotten and I thought there was nothing further about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
What occurred was, the hon. gentleman made some assertions with respect to a speech which the hon. member from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) was alleged to have made somewhere in the 12 m. county of Victoria. The hon.
. member from Annapolis denied having made those statements. It was then the duty of my hon. friend to say that he was bound to accept the .statements made by the hon. member for Annapolis from his place in this House. My hon. [DOT] friend would not do that. The hon. member for Annapolis, getting a little incensed, made use of a most improper expression and almost immediately afterwards withdrew it. My hon. friend is bound to accept the statement made by the hon. member for Annapolis in answer to the statement as to the remarks alleged to have been made by him at a meeting held at Victoria.
I have already stated to the Chair that any conventionalities required to maintain the dignity of Parliament, 1 have complied with. That is as far as I shall go or can be expected to go.
I understand my hon. friend to say that he accepts my statement.
What I have written I have written.
I do not think I am unreasonable in insisting that the gentleman do that in language we can all understand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Am I to understand
that the hon. gentleman accepts the statement of the hon. member for Annapolis when he says that he has not used such words?

I am sorry that it is
so extremely difficult for me to make myself understood. I understand the rule of the House to require that, if a certain hon. member makes a statement to another and that other hon. member denies it, that denial must be accepted. It has been said a thousand times by hon. members on both sides during my years of occupancy of a seat in this House. I accept the statement in a parliamentary sense. That has never been questioned. Whatever is necessary , to be done in a parliamentary sense to satisfy the dignity of the hon. member for Annapolis has already been done by me in a parliamentary sense. Why should not the same language be accepted from me as has been over and over again accepted by the Speaker and by the Chair that compliance in a parliamentary sense with the conventionalities of debate in this House should be satisfied? I have endeavoured to satisfy them and that should be the end of it.
That is absolutely satisfactory.

I want to refer' to the
dismissal of Lloyd Charles Dakin, former lighthouse keeper at Grand Harbour in the province of New Brunswick. On the 17th of July, 1912, Mr. Dakin received a letter from Mr. Hallett, acting deputy minister as follows:
Sir,_I have to inform you that by Order In
Council of the 17th March, 1912, your services as keeper of the light and hand fog-horn at Grand Harbour, N.B., have been dispensed with, owing to offensive political partisanship, and Mr. Fred. J. Martin has been directed to take temporary charge of the light, to whom you will give up possession of all Government property under your care when required.
I am, sir,
Your obedient servant,
J. Hallett.
That was followed up by a letter of the 23rd of July from Mr. Flood who was acting as the agent of the department. Shortly after that a telegram was sent to Mr. Hartt, the member for the constituency as follows:
T. Mr. Hartt, M.P.,
Member for Charlotte county.
We as citizens of Grand Harbour do, to our knowledge, know that Lloyd Dakin has never
taken any part, aside from casting his personal vote, in any provincial election.
.	(Sgd) D. H. Daggett.
Isaac Newton.
Owen Green.
Wesley Newton.
C. A. Newton.
And three other names were added by telephone, Edward Russell, Chester Russell and Arnold Russell. All of these purport to be strong Conservatives. The next thing was a letter of the 31st of July' from Mr. Flood expressing surprise that Mr. Dakin had refused to give up the position and a letter of the 7th of August acknowledging that Mr. Dakin had complied with the requirement of the department and given up the position. But Mr. Dakin did not seem satisfied to accept the decision of the department, feeling that he had not done any wrong. So, he wrote the following letter:
Grand Harbour, August 17, 1912. Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Dear Sir-Yours of the 7 th received informing me that my case would be investigated. Would you please let me know when the investigation will take place.
Mr. Hartt, the member for the county, is now at home.
The charge is false, and I can easily prove it, and the whole thing is the work of two or three persons.
Respectfully yours,
Lloyd C. Dakin.
On the 11th of September there is the acknowledgment of the Deputy Minister, stating that in the great rush of departmental work it is impossible to give it immediate consideration, but that later on consideration will be given. On the 24th of September he received an official letter signed by C . Stanton, assistant Deputy Minister, which is as follows:
Referring to your letter of the 17th ultimo, in reply to departmental letter of the 7th August, 1912, respecting your request for an investigation in the case of your dismissal from the position of the light and hand fog horn at Grand Harbour, New Brunswick, I have to state that in the departmental letter referred to you were merely informed that your request for an investigation would receive the consideration of the department.
The charge for which your services were dispensed with was the statement in writing of Mr. T. A. Hartt, M.P., that you attended one of his meetings and tried to annoy him; that you remained after the meeting closed and endeavoured to impress your views in his presence on the people before they left the hall.
I am, sir,
Yours obedient servant,
C. Stanton,
Assistant Deputy Minister. Mr. Lloyd C. Dakin,
Grand Harbour, New Brunswick.

On this Mr. Dakin answers as follows:
27th September.
Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Replying to your letter of September 24, in regard to the charge for which my services were dispensed with as keeper of Grand Harbour light, that I had tried to annoy Mr. T. A. Hartt, M.P., at his meetings and at the close tried to impress my views in his presence on the people before they left the hall-I would like to say that since receiving my dismissal I have talked, with Mr. Hartt personally, and he acknowledged to me that he had made a mistake-that I was not the man-and he had been wrongly impressed and also promised to do what he could to rectify it.
While in the service, I did not attend any political meetings, and more than that never took part in politics in my life, and upon my dismissal sent Mr. Hartt a statement to that effect, signed by prominent Conservatives, among whom was Mr. Issac Newton, whom Mr. Hazen, Minister of Marine and Fisheries, knows to be one of the oldest and most respected Conservatives of Grand Manan.
Trusting that you will make further investigation.
I remain,
Yours respectfully,
Lloyd C. Dakin.
Does the Minister of Marine and Fisheries recollect the man?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, I know Mr. Newton very well.

On the 1st of October there is an official acknowledgment to that letter. On the 20th of October there is another letter written by Mr. Dakin to the department which simply refers to some conversation he had with Mr. Hartt. I have next a letter from Mr. Hartt himself. I am glad the hon. gentleman is here; I did not wish to make any reference to this matter until he was in his place:
St. Andrews, N.B., October 16, 1912. Lloyd C. Dakin,
Grand Harbour, Grand Manan.
Dear Sir,-I have written the department at Ottawa telling my mistake and clearing you of the charge.
I will have to let the appointment go as it is for the present. I tried to explain my position to you when I saw you here, and I hope you will understand me and that we may be friends. We cannot see into the future. I may be able to do something for you some time.
Yours truly,
T. A. Hartt.
I should say that was a very diplomatic letter. It holds out the olive branch, it expresses the belief that there will be other positions at their disposal-altogether I do not know that I find very much fault with it. The hon. gentleman was in a rather unpleasant position, and he tried to 
let the man down as easily as he could. However, that did not suit this official, and on the 19th of October he again addressed the deputy minister:
I have just received a letter from Mr. T. A. Hartt, M.P., saying he had written the department at Ottawa, telling his mistake, and clearing me of the charge, but he has not seemed to make an effort towards getting back my former position, which was taken from me on account of this false accusation. Now being cleared, would you please let me know definitely whether I -am to be reinstated or not.
Yours respectfully,
Lloyd C. Dal.'.i.
There is a letter of Mr. Hartt, but as it is practically along the same lines it is not necessary to read it, unless the hon. gentleman himself thinks it should be read.
I think there has been quite enough.

I have only two or three more. There was an official acknowledgment of Mr. Dakins' letter:
I beg to acknowledge receipt of yours of the 19th inst. with further reference to your removal from the position of keeper of the Grand Harbour light. The department will, at the very earliest opportunity, give every possible consideration to the representations that you have made from time to time, and as soon as a definite decision has been reached you will be advised.
On the 16th of November, Mr. Dakin addressed himself again to the deputy minister as follows:
Would you please let me know the decision of the department in regard to whether I am to be reinstated or not at Grand Harbour light? I cannot understand why I am not reinstated, since I have been cleared of the charge, for Mr. T. A. Hart,, ivl.p., wrote me he had written the department clearing me. I would like, if possible, to have an answer before the last of next week, as I am very unsettled for winter.
Yours respectfully,
Lloyd C. Dakin.
In reply to this he received the following:
Dear Sir,-Replying to your letter of the 16th ultimo, I am to observe that I have but little to add to my letter to you of the 29th of October. It is represented to the department that there was sufficient warrant for your removal from office, and consequently the proposal to reinstate you is not being entertained.
Yours very truly,
A. Johnston,
Deputy Minister.
The man naturally feels very much aggrieved at the treatment he has received, and in order to put the matter in as fair a manner as possible, he has furnished me

with an affidavit. I will not read it all, because he practically recites the burden of the correspondence I have read. This affidavit was sworn to on the 26th of March-last week-and it is in part as follows:
That the charges made against me were false ; that I have never taken a part in politics in my life other than to cast my vote; that I was not present at any political meeting addressed by Mr. Hartt, M.P., or by any other person; that I have never attended a political meeting of any kind either in connection with Dominion or provincial politics since the date of my appointment as keeper of said light and hand foghorn and np to the time of my dismissal from said position, except once.
That is the whole case so far as I know. I do not know this gentleman personal^ at all. But I bring the facts before the committee. I have read nothing but official documents and letters which Mr. Dakin swears are true copies of those he sent to the department. It would seem from these that there is no doubt the man was dismissed from office under misapprehension on the part of the hon. member for the county (Mr. Hartt).
I have read the letter of the hon. member for Charlotte in which he says that he is mistaken, expresses regret for what 0as happened and holds out the olive branch of the possibility that he may at some time in the future be able to rectify the wrong that has been done. But what the discharged official cannot understand is why the minister, when it was found that this man was not guilty of the offence with which he was originally charged, said sometime afterwards: it is true that you are innocent of that charge, but there are other charges against you. I have a right to request the minister to tell the committee what were the other ctiarges upon which he felt that he was justified in dismissing this man-because the man was dismissed on some charge other than that made by the member for the county. I feel that- this case is an exemplification of the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite are carrying to the extreme the doctrine of ' to the victors belong the spoils.'

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My recollection of the
matter is that this man was dismissed at the request and upon the responsibility of the member for the county. During the last two sessions it has been stated time and again in this House by the right hon. gentleman who was formerly Prime Minister that when a member supporting the
Government takes the responsibility of asking for the dismissal of an official it is quite right and proper that the department should dismiss him. The right hon. gentleman laid down a different rule to apply to cases where the man was dismissed upon the recommendation of some person who was not a member of this House. I do not remember the other facts in connection with the matter, and as it comes under the Marine Department and we are discussing to-night the fisheries branch, I have not before me the information which my hon. friend asks for. I shall be glad to show my hon. friend all the papers in Tegard to the matter.

The facts in connection with this matter are quite fresh in my memory. When a person makes a mistake I suppose the best thing for him to do is to acknowledge it as soon as possible. I was interrupted at a meeting at Grand Harbour, and I was quite sure, from what was said by persons who were present, that the man who interrupted me was the lighthouse keeper. I had some correspondence with the young man, and he came up to see me-a very decent young fellow, too. He told me that he had never taken part in an election and that he had not interrupted me at the meeting. When I saw him I knew that he was Tight, and that he was not the man. Finding that l had made an error, I said that I would try to rectify it, and that I would look into the matter carefully. He assured me at the time that he was quite in sympathy with me politically; in fact, I was led to believe that he was a good Conservative, and. I was probably the more easily led to this belief because I found that he was a particular friend of my son-in-law, who came with him to see me and to say a word on his behalf. They had been friends for years; I thought it was quite possible that the young man might be entirely in sympathy with me, and that I had made a big mistake. But it is always well to look around before you acknowledge that you are entirely in the wrong. I looked into the matter and endeavoured to find out whether or not he had been an active political partisan, and it was some little time before I got on the right track. Finally, I found out on good authority that he bet money against me in the election-and of course he lost his money. When a man bets money against a candidate at an election, it is a

*pretty sure indication of political partisanship. Having recommended his dismissal, and having named another man for his position, I had gone so far that I found myself in a difficult position. 1 could not turn around and reinstate him on the spot, but, in any case, in view of the facts that I had ascertained, I said: Here is proof positive that this man took active part in an election; he could not do more than bet money against one oi the candidates. Accordingly, I recommended to the department that his dismissal be sustained, and that the man who had been appointed should continue to occupy his position. The matter has stood that way ever since, and I think it will stand that way. Of course, I did feel at the time somewhat sorry that the young man had been ill-used, but when I came to look into the matter, wben I found that his professions were not exactly up to the mark; that he had taken part in elections and was not as friendly towards me as he professed to be, I came to the conclusion that no harm had been done in disimissing him. With regard to the papers which have been read, no mention was made in them of the circumstance which I have mentioned with regard to the betting. I am somewhat surprised that the gentleman has brought the matter up at all, because when I wrote him and explained that I had obtained this evidence of his having taken part in the election, the correspondence stopped at once, and I heard nothing more about the matter until these papers were banded to me and I was asked to look them over.

The statement which
has been made by the hon. member for Charlotte goes to show the extent to which the present Government are determined to go in order to get a man's political scalp on every possible occasion. We have heard a confession the like of which is very seldom made in this House. I respect the hon. member for Charlotte for the frank confession which he has made, but it only proves that this man had to go, and, once he was out, no matter whether or not there was evidence against him, he had to stay out.
One thing that must strike every member is the manner in which my friends opposite break every law of the political decalogue when it is necessary to get a man's position, if they want it. The minister says that it is the well recognized rule that the departments take the word of a member

of this House but do not take the word of a man who is not a member. I have spoken to the Minister of Customs about one official in my constituency, but that is the only occasion that I have interfered in any way in reference to retaining or dismissing any official; but they have been fired right and left, fired on investigations in which evidence was not forthcoming, hut they have been fired just the same; and fired without investigation simply on the letter of the gentleman who opposed me in the campaign. Our friends may as well admit that when they want a man's position they take it, and not try to get behind a rule which is more honoured in the breach than in the observance.

The minister has not yet answered the inquiry of the hon. member for North Cape Breton. If Fraser is an employee of the department and did what he is charged with doing, what position is the minister going to take in regard to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall look into the matter and see what action I think the circumstances of the case would justify.

That is very indefinite. The minister should investigate this clear and definite charge against this man of doing a disreputable thing. The practice has been when a charge of disreputable conduct has been made against any official, that the minister of the department concerned would at once frankly say that he would have the matter investigated and do what was right.
What are the regulations of the department in regard to building fishways and dams?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was not in the House when we discussed the Bill consolidating the Fisheries Act. I explained then that we are making certain changes, so that in cases where fishways are placed in old dams the department pay one-half the cost. If the department orders a fishway put in a dam and it is done at the expense of the owner, the plans being approved by the department, and it turns out that the fishway is not effective and another style is ordered, under the present law the owner has to pay the whole expense; we have changed that so that the department pays the cost of the new fishway ordered.

In case a fishway is washed out after the owner has paid one-half its

cost, does the department pay one-half the cost of replacing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Where the fishway is being constructed at the same time as the dam is built, the extra cost is trifling, and that, of course, would apply in the case where a dam was completely washed away. It would, of course, depend on the circumstances of the case. I think a case occurred in the hon. gentleman's county last year where we paid one-half the cost.
The new Act will not change that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The changes make it better in the interest of the owners of the property.
Canadian Fisheries Museum, $16,000.

I had the pleasure of visiting tfiis exhibit last week, and I think it is a credit to the department and to the gentlemen instrumental in having it established. It is a great improvement on the old exhibit.
Fisheries patrol service, $160,000.
I wish to refer to the steamer Niobe's visit to Yarmouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That has really nothing to do with this. It should be taken up when the Naval Estimates are before the House which will be in the course of a few days.
Do these boats include those employed in connection with the lobster hatcheries.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The boats my hon. friend
refers to are, as a rule, small boats rented from private individuals. Perhaps I had better explain the difference between the. fisheries protection boats and the fisheries patrol boats. The fisheries protection boats are used for the purpose of protecting Canadian waters from people who have no business to come in there to fish such boats as the Canada and the Curlew, for instance. They are supposed to keep our waters within the three-mile limit for our own fishermen. Those boats are under the control of the Naval Service Department. The fisheries patrol boats are the boats that my hon. friend refers to and the small boats that enforce the regulations within the three-mile limit.

I have in mind the small
steamer Davis employed around the county of Richmond collecting lobster seed from the different hatcheries to be deposited at the hatchery at Arichat.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: She is one of the patrol boats. She was used for that purpose before the patrol season opened. The Curlew belongs to the Fisheries Protection Service.
There Is a large increase in this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The increase is accounted for in this way: Seven new patrol boats have been placed in commission in British Columbia, the cost of maintaining which is estimated to be $25,000. A more expensive boat is to be commissioned for the enforcement of the regulations among the islands and along the coast of Charlotte county, N.B. The cost of maintenance of that boat will probably be $1,000 more than the previous boat. Then in order to prevent illegal lobster fishing off the coast of New Brunswick it will be necessary to build some boats. That makes up the extra money.
What is the size of these boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are small gasoline
boats.
Fishery patrol boats for the Atlantic coast, $40,000.
What'provision is made for protecting the coast from the encroachment of American fishermen?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is done by the fisheries protection fleet which is under the control of the Naval Department. The boats in the fisheries protection fleet are such boats as the Canadian-that is the best one-and the Curlew, the Constance, and boats of that character. There are a number of them in British Columbia.

In the spring of the
year when the cod and haddock fishing is on, we look for protection all along the coast of New Brunswick, especially in the northern part of the province. In the season of mackerel fishing it is exceedingly difficult to keep American vessels outside the limit. A trip by one of our Government steamers once in two weeks is absolutely inadequate.' American poachers should realize that protection is close at hand and that they cannot poach with impunity.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are not particularly
well supplied with suitable boats, but we are fairly well supplied. Last year when the American fleet started out we kept one of our boats along with them all the time to watch the American fishermen. If they came within the three-mile limit they



would either be driven out or arrested. Very few complaints reached the department last year in regard to poaching within the limits. The Canada is the best of our boats on the Atlantic coast, hut hardly one of them can be trusted in a heavy gale. There are times when those boats ought to go out to sea, but it is not safe for them to do so. The conditions on the British Columbia coast were far worse, but this year we have had two new boats built, with the money voted two years ago for use there. We will not be put to the expense of chartering boats as we were before and we will have a very much better service there. It may be necessary next session to ask Parliament for an appropriation for getting some better boats on the Atlantic.

How are these boats
built?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By tender and contract.

I would like to ask the minister if the tenders will be the same as the tenders that my hon. friend referred to in a former discussion. He assured the House on a former occasion that tenders were	asked	for	in the	caseof Fred. S.	Heans	of St. John	forsome work that was done for his department. I was	told by	the	minister	thattenders were asked for	and	that the	contract was let in the usual way. When I put the question on the Order Paper I found that tenders were not asked for from the public by advertising in the newspapers but that a number of letters were sent to some of the friends of my hon. friend inviting them to put in tenders and that in that way the selection was made. I put the five cases of Fred. S. Heans, St. John; Burns and Kellebar, Halifax; Union Foundry Works, St. John; Geo. T. Davie and Son, Levis and the Canadian Import Company on the Order Paper and in every case I got the same answer from the minister that there had been no tender in the newspapers but that the usual practice of the department was observed of asking these people to tender. We all know what that means-that the minister only asks his political friends to tender. I trust that in the case of this boat everybody will be given an opportunity and that tenders will be asked for in public. There does not seem to be any advertising in these cases.
I was very much surprised, upon taking these five cases, to get the same answer from the minister that there had been no [Mr. Hazen.J
advertisements published calling upon the public to put in tenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The cost would be a great deal higher if we were to do in every case as my hon. friend suggests. I told my hon. friend that everything is done on the boats themselves and so it is. The people who do this work are known in the community, notices are sent to them from the agencies, they put in their tenders and .in some cases a tender is not half as much as the highest tender put in, showing the nature of the competition that takes place. In the case of boats of this sort, where the work can be done at one place as well as another, at Quebec as well as at Halifax or St. John, advertisements are put in the public newspapers, but in cases where the work has to be done at a certain place, such as repairs to a ship, it is a waste* of time and of money to advertise in the newspapers for tenders. We always get competition. For these boats, tenders will be asked by advertisement in the public press all over the country. That was done at the time the last boats were purchased and the lowest tenderer was a firm at Dartmouth, F. E. Williams & Company, to whom the contract was awarded.
To provide for an exhibit of fresh and cured food fish at the Toronto annual exhibition, $15,000.
Did the minister carry out the idea that we talked of last year at the Toronto exhibition about having a restaurant?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We tried to do it but we could not get room in the exhibition buildings. The directors could not give us a place to have the kitchen and restaurant. But the exhibition, in spite of that, was a very great success. The directors awarded us a gold medal and the newspapers spoke in very high terms of the exhibit. This year we are asking for $15,000, an extra $5,000, and we are going to try and carry out the idea of having a restaurant even if we have to have it outside of the main building.

Where does the department
purchase the fish for the Toronto exhibition?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
From all parts of Canada, British Columbia, the Atlantic and the lakes.
Salaries, building and maintenance of fishbreeding establishments, $400,000.

243t
May I suggest that this item be held and the rest may all pass?
Has application been made by the Crui'des Association in Yarmouth for the establishment of a fish haltchery at that place?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The superintendent of
fisheries tells me that he had some recollection of a request received a month or two ago asking that a fish hatchery be established at Yarmouth. The matter is in the department. We have bad a number of applications from all parts of Canada for these hatcheries, a great many more than our vote will enable us to establish. We have been proceeding in the last few years, however, and no doubt in the future further ones will be established.
I gather from the remarks of the minister that there is not very much chance of the Guides Association getting a hatchery.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: You should never get discouraged about these things.

Has the minister considered
the establishment of a lobster pond at Lower West Pubnico? An official of the department has made three visits down there and I understand he has reported in favour of the proposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We have come to the conclusion not to establish any more ponds anywhere until more thorough experiments have been carried on with the ponds that we have at the present time.

There is a natural pond at
Lower West Pubnico and an official of the department has reported favourably upon it on three different occasions. That property can be bought for $1,000; yet, the hon. gentleman went 'to Long Beach, St. Mary's, Digby, and established a lobster pond that was a failure.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has not proved a failure. We have just finished it.

That property could have been purchased for $1,000; and with an expenditure of one or two thousand dollars more, it could have been fitted up and been a great accommodation to the fishermen in that whole section of the county of Yarmouth. Instead of the minister wasting the money of the people of this country in paying $20,400 for property assessed for $350, he should have looked into the matter a little more closely and purchased the pond in Yarmouth county at Lower West Pubnico. The lobster fishermen on the coast of Yarmouth as well as on the northern part of the coast of Shelburne are entitled to a proper lobster pond especially when it can be purchased at so much lower a price than has been paid to this friend of the present Administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Perhaps there is not time enough to-night to discuss this matter fully. My hon. friend has referred, however, to a few of tire papers on the file I laid before the House. The hon. gentleman quotes from a report of Professor Prince with regard to this pond and its suitability for lobsters, in which he states, that because of certain fresh water catch he does not think it suitable for that purpose. If my hon. friend had looked a little longer, he would have found a second memorandum of Professor Prince saying that the water had been diverted from the pond and, that being the case, it was well suited for the 1 a.m. purpose of a lobster pond. My hon. friend, if he had wanted to be fair, would have stated that to the House. He did not do so. Either he had not read the whole file through or else he had no desire to state the facts fairly to this committee.
In regard to the price, my hon. friend will find in the return the statement from Mr. Brunei to the effect that we could not have duplicated that pond and the work that was there for the sum of $10,000, the amount we paid for it. It will also appear from the record of the proceedings, which, I think, are on the file, that while Mr. Brunei on one page spoke of $5,000, he did it at the time that we were dickering for the property and he thought, by making that statement, it would be possible for us to 'buy the property at a cheaper price. But he stated that that pond and the work there could not be duplicated for $10,000. That is the statement of a responsible officer of my department.
It cost $20 400.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly. There has been work done on the pond afterwards. The pond is -worth every dollar of the money' that has been spent on it.1 The money has been economically spent under the direction of the engineers of the department in whom I have confidence and who have spent the money to good advantage. [DOT]
My hon. friend has made merry about the number of lobsters. The pond was not ready for the lobsters last year. A great many more lobsters will be put in the pond during this and coming years. The pond has been purchased for the purpose of experimenting with lobsters in order to see whether something cannot be done towards replenishing the lobster fisheries along the coast of Nova Scotia.
There is not a single transaction in connection with it that we are not prepared to justify or that we do not believe have been in the public interest. Nothing has been done by me except after careful investigation and report by the permanent officers of the department, who were there long before I became minister. Having confidence in their reports and in the integrity of these officers, I believe that everything has been done honestly and properly, and that the result will be to develop the lobster fishery along the shores of Nova Scotia to the great advantage of the people.

I would ask the. minister if he thinks this statement of Mr. Brunei's conduct in this matter is calculated to elevate him in the estimation of the public as a conscientious officer. Will he admit that Mr. Brunei was right if he made his report merely with the idea of beating down the owner of this property? I do not know if the minister quite appreciates the statement he made; but it appears to me that if the officers of his department go out to estimate the value of property it should be to give an honest opinion of the value and to direct the minister as to the course he should take. But if these officers base their estimate of value of property to be purchased on the ground which the minister indicates, then I think these reports are very much less valuable than they ought to be. I trust that Mr. Brunei did not estimate the value of the property at $5,000 solely for the purpose of representing to the owner that it was less valuable to the department than it really was. If the statement given by the minister is to be accepted as given, then I think every criticism directed by the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law), is very

amply borne out. Here was the property assessed at $350 before it was purchased. Here is the report of Mr. Brunei, that it was only worth $5,000. Here also is the report of Professor Prince that the property was not suitable for the purposes of a lobster pond. The minister states that subsequently streams of fresh water were diverted from the pond, making it suitable for the purposes for which it was purchased, and I doubt not that this diversion was accomplished by the expenditure of $10,400 after the Government had paid $10,000 for the property. Professor Prince also stated that it was too much exposed to the rays of the sun to be suitable for breeding lobsters. It has not been stated that they diverted the rays of the sun by means of this expenditure, but the amount would seem to indicate that that also had been attempted. Of course, the whole value of the property for a lobster pond would depend upon it being a sheltered place and protected from the rays of the sun, for there is nothing more fatal to young lobsters than high temperature of the water in which they dwell. If this pond were open to the direct rays of the sun it would make it unsuitable for this purpose. As I stated, I trust the minister will remove from the committee the impression he gave as to Mr. Brunei s conscientiousness when he made his report.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is it desired that this item should stand ?
I think it would be better to let that stand.
The next item is ' inspection of canned fish.' I think that ought to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That matter has been under the administration of the Department of Agriculture, but the inspection of canned fish has never been actually carried out. It was considered this year that the Department of Marine and Fisheries had better deal with that subject, and so the administration of that portion of the Act was placed under the Fisheries Department. Details are now being considered.
I think a good deal of discussion will develop on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Then, let the item for fish breeding establishments go through.
As it is going through, I desire to ask, is the department doing anything about stocking fresh water lakes, say in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. gentleman has in mind the sporting fish, such as
trout. There is a fish hatchery at Bedford where such fry can be obtained, and one at Middleton in the county of Annapolis. Of course, at the salmon hatcheries other fish can be hatched. As a rule people make application for the fry of these sporting fish, paying so much a thousand, and it is distributed in this way as far as it will go.
There is a lake at the back of the town in which I live and

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is it private property?

No, it is a lake about three miles long and a mile wide. The only ownership is that the town of Sydney Mines gets its water from the lake. There is a desire on the part of the people that this lake should be stocked, and I think it would be well worth the experiment to put fry in it. There is a fish that flourishes abundantly in the lakes of Newfoundland, called the rainbow trout, a beautiful fish and very game. I would request that the minister consider putting some fry into that lake.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There will be some fry
available from the Margaree hatchery and some of it might be put in the lake mentioned. I will ask the superintendent to make a note olit.

Can the hon.
minister give the committee an idea of the number of trout put in that Margaree hatchery?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell the number this year. Arrangements are being made to catch and impound trout, so that in future years we shall have a large supply of eggs for the hatcheries.
Where does the minister expect to get this trout?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the Margaree river.
At what season?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will have to be got and impounded in the early part of +he summer, and the spawn taken from them during the spawning season.
What has been the result of the work of the Shad Commission, which was appointed two or three years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That commission was appointed before this Government took office, but I shall be glad to get a copy of the report and send it to my hon. friend.
What is the Government doing now along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When fishery items were before the committee the hon. member foi Oarleton made some remarks about certain fishery overseers in his county, and he gave the name of one official who, he thought, was violating the law. The hon. gentleman stated that Mr. Parker and another guardian whose name he did not mention were noted poachers, and obtained their employment merely to enable them to carry on salmon fishing in the St. John river. I have a memorandAm here in regard to the matter, which is as follows:
The inspector of fisheries was immediately asked for a report, and he replied that not only had he given strict instructions to the guardians to prevent illegal fishing, but that their diaries did not indicate that such had been going on. Moreover, at his request, none of them had applied for salmon fishery licenses to enable them to fish during the legal season.
Me has procured declarations from each one who was employed last year, Mr. Parker inclusive, from which it will be observed that they each state that they did not fish illegally since they were appointed, nor did they knowingly let any one else do so illegally.
Mr. Harrison, the inspector, has reported that he cannot find any evidence whatever of illegal fishing having been carried on by any of these officials. Mr. Newcombe Parker made a declaration in the matte as follows: I,
I,	Newcombe Parker, a former special guardian of fisheries, appointed by the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for Canada, on duty for the protection of the fisheries in the county of Carleton, N.B., from the 15th day IMr. Boggie.]
of May, to the 15th day of September, 1913, do solemnly make oath and say that I did not fish with a net, nor by any other method, illegally, since my first appointment as fishery officer in 1912, and up to the present date, neither have I knowingly permitted illegal fishing, by any method, in any of the waters in the district for which I was appointed, covering the time of my appointments, and which times I was a fishery officer, viz: May 15, 1912, and May 15 to September 15, 1913. So help me God.
Here is a letter from Frank O. Parker to Mr. Harrison:
I wish to state outside of this enclosed declaration that I have never caught a salmon in the St. John river in my life. I have never owned a net nor fished with one in the St. John river or anywhere else.
There are similar statements from Russell Boyer, Robert Squires and John O. Arnold. These I believe are all the guardians employed there, and, as I say, Mr. Harrison -says we told him to make the strictest possible inquiry into the whole matter. I shall show the instructions to my hon. friend if he desires to see them. Harrison says he can find no evidence of anything of the sort and Parker makes his affidavit denying it. If my hon. friend can give me the names of his informants so that we can send Harrison to them we would regard it as a confidential communication. We would tell the inspector to see these people and find out if he could get any evidence to show that my hon. friend was correct and not misled by incorrect information in the charge he made before the House. We have done all we can to ferret the matter out. So far as I know Harrison is a competent official, he has been there for many years and he says he can get no evidence and that his belief is the law is pretty well enforced.

I need not say that I did not myself see Mr. Parker poaching; but I would not have made such a statement if I bad not had pretty good grounds for doing so. I have it on the evidence of men living at Bristol where he lives that it is a common thing, in season and out of season.
I do not know that I have information of men who have seen Parker himself fishing but they have seen his relatives, and it is well known that poaching is going on continually. I shall try to get the information for the minister. Probably what has been said here will make Mr. Parker and his relatives more careful.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If Parker has done this or has winked at it, he should not be allowed to continue in office.
Progress reported.

On motion of Mr. Hazen, the House adjourned at 1.30 a.m., Saturday.
Monday, April 6, 1914.
